Figure 1 on page 7 above demonstrates what type of moveable coupling member infringes the claims of the patents. As noted supra, Zhuhai Kingly asserts that the Kingly Toner Cartridge does not infringe these patents because its article does not possess the inclining, moveable coupling member as recited in the relevant patent claims.  According to Zhuhai Kingly, the Kingly Toner Cartridge has a coupling member that does not move in its own plane or perpendicular to the same axis as the drum unit, but is firmly set in the flange.  An examination by CBP of a sample of the Kingly Toner Cartridge, as depicted in Figures 5 and 6 (page 9 above), confirms Zhuhai Kingly’s assertion.  The coupling member in Figures 7 and 8 (page 9 above) uses a lever mechanism to push out two protrusions that engage the drive shaft of the printer to rotate the photosensitive drum when in use.    Because the Kingly Toner Cartridge does not possess a coupling member that is moveable between first and second positions in the manner recited in the relevant claims, these articles do not meet all the claim elements of any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, or ’008 patents, or any of the claims that depend therefrom..  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Kingly’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.“Angle of Inclination of Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsIn addition to the claim element that requires that a toner cartridge possess a moveable coupling member as described above, such a coupling member’s axis must also pivot within a 20 degree to 60-degree range from the axis of the drum unit.  This claim element is found in the following claims:  claim 160 of the ’278 patent; claim 171 of the ’564 patent; claim 23 of the ’215 patent, and claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent.As described above, the coupling on the Kingly Toner Cartridge does not pivot at all.  Rather, the coupling on the Kingly Toner Cartridge is set in place in the flange coaxial with the axis of the drum unit and it is the two protrusions inside the coupling that are the only things that move (they are pushed out of the coupling).  Because the coupling does not pivot at all it does not create any angle of inclination that falls within 20 degrees to 60 degrees (or any degrees) from that of the drum unit’s axis and thus do not meet the claim elements of the asserted claims listed in the preceding paragraph of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents that have an angle of inclination requirement.  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Kingly’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.The ’090 PatentIndependent claim 1 of the ’090 patent recites an electrophotographic photosensitive drum unit that includes a cylinder and a drum flange provided at one end of the cylinder.  The drum flange includes at least two projections that are provided inside of the drum flange and that project radially inwardly of the drum flange.  Claim 1 further recites, in relevant part, that “each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.”As noted above in section I(C), Zhuhai Kingly withdrew a portion of its non-infringement argument relating to the flange of the Kingly Toner Cartridge in response to a request by Canon.  Nevertheless, Canon indicates that it does not dispute Zhuhai Kingly’s remaining argument that, on the Kingly Toner Cartridge, “the projection in its drum flange extends less inwardly at a position further from the photosensitive drum that it does at a position closer to the drum.”  (See E-mail from Michael Sandonato to Christine Lehman and William Wittwer (Jan. 5, 2018).  A review of the schematics in figures 9 and 10 (page 10 above) of the Kingly Toner Cartridge drum flanges confirms the Kingly Toner Cartridge possesses a configuration in which the projection in its drum flange extends less inwardly at a position further from the photosensitive drum that it does at a position closer to the drum.  By contrast, claim 1 requires the opposite configuration, one in which each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.  As such, the Kingly Toner Cartridge does not meet all the elements of claim 1 of the ’090 patent, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.Therefore, based on the evidence in the record, we find that Zhuhai Kingly has met its burden to show that the Kingly Toner Cartridge does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.   Thus, the Kingly Toner Cartridge is outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.
sections.HOLDING: The Kingly Toner Cartridge manufactured by Zhuhai Kingly Technology Co., Ltd. does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.  As such, Kingly Toner Cartridges are not subject to exclusion from entry for consumption into the United States, entry for consumption from a foreign-trade zone, or withdrawal from a warehouse for consumption.This decision is limited to the facts set forth herein.  If Zhuhai Kingly manufactures or imports toner cartridges and drum units whose designs differs from the embodiment described above, or if future importations vary from the facts stipulated to herein, this decision shall not be binding on CBP as provided for in 19 C.F.R. §§177.2(b)(1), (2), and (4), and §§ 177.9(b)(1) and (2).					Sincerely,					Charles R. Steuart, Chief					Intellectual Property Rights Branch

We hold that the toner cartridge at issue in this ruling letter is not subject to the general exclusion order (“GEO”) issued by the U.S. International Trade Commission (“ITC” or “Commission”) in Investigation No. 337-TA-918 (“the ’918 investigation”).  This ruling letter is the result of an inter partes proceeding administered by CBP.  The inter partes proceeding involved the two parties with a direct and demonstrable interest in the question presented by the ruling request: your clients, Topjet Technology Co., Ltd., Maxwell Image Ltd., and E-Z Ink, Inc. (collectively, “Requesters” or “Topjet”) and Canon Inc. of Japan, Canon U.S.A., Inc. of Melville, New York, and Canon Virginia, Inc. of Newport News, Virginia (collectively, “Canon”).BACKGROUND:A. 	Rule 177 Proceeding before the IPR Branch	On December 22, 2017, Requesters submitted a letter (“Ruling Request”) requesting an administrative ruling pursuant to 19 C.F.R. part 177 as to whether certain toner cartridges (“the Topjet toner cartridges”) manufactured by Topjet Technology Co., Ltd., imported by E-Z Ink, Inc., and sold by Maxwell Image Ltd. would be subject to the GEO issued by the ITC in the ’918 investigation.  See Ruling Request at 1-2 and 11, Dec. 22, 2017.  Specifically, the Ruling Request seeks a ruling with respect to the 505 series toner cartridge (“505 toner cartridge”).  Topjet submitted a sample of the 505 toner cartridge with the Ruling Request.On January 19, 2018, Topjet indicated that a copy of the Ruling Request was provided to Canon and requested return of the samples provided to CBP to provide Cannon an opportunity to review the Topjet toner cartridges.  See E-mail from David Farnum, counsel for Topjet, to William Wittwer, attorney-advisor at CBP (Jan. 19, 2018). On February 2, 2018, Canon responded to the Ruling Request, indicating that it reviewed the Topjet toner cartridges, and that it “does not object to the requested rulings that the Topjet cartridges do not fall within the scope of the GEO issued in Investigation No. 337-TA-918, but it disagrees with one aspect of Requesters’ arguments…”  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).  Specifically, Canon stated:The disagreement relates to claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 8,676,090 (“the ’090 patent”).  This claim requires, among other things, a drum flange that includes “at least two projections provided inside of the drum flange and projected radially inwardly of the drum flange, with a space diametrically between the two projections.”  The claim further requires that “each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.”  Requesters assert that the Topjet cartridges do not infringe the claims of the ’090 patent because the cartridges do not have flanges with projections that project radially inward toward the center of the flange.  Canon disagrees, and believes that the flange on each of the subject cartridges includes at least two projections that project radially inward.  Requesters further assert that there are no projections that are “closer together farther from the drum,” i.e., that project radially inwardly to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder.  Canon does not dispute this latter point, and accordingly does not dispute Requesters’ ultimate conclusion with respect to the ’090 patent. Id.  Canon further stated that “[p]rovided that Requesters withdraw their argument with respect to the ’090 patent that the flanges in the Topjet cartridges lack inward projections and/or CBP limits its ruling to the undisputed part of Requesters’ arguments (i.e., that each drum flange does not have projections that project inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than they do at a position closer to the cylinder), we see no reason for Canon to participate in this proceeding.”  Id.  In response to Canon, Topjet agreed to: (i) withdraw its argument that the flanges in the proposed Topjet toner cartridges lack inward projections, and (ii) limit the basis for its ruling request to the argument that its proposed cartridges have “no projections that are ‘closer together farther from the drum,’ i.e., that project radially inwardly to a greater extent at a positon farther from the cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder.”  See E-mail from David Farnum to William Wittwer, Michael Sandonato, and Edmund Haughey (Feb. 4, 2018).In view of Topjet’s withdrawal of all arguments disputed by Canon and Canon’s clear indication that it does not dispute any of the remaining arguments, no additional briefing or oral argument was needed by CBP in this inter partes proceeding to reach a determination regarding the questions presented in the Ruling Request.  For the reasons discussed below, we hold that the Topjet 505 toner cartridge is not subject to the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.B.  	Investigation No. 337-TA-9181.  	Procedural HistoryThe Commission instituted the ’918 investigation on June 12, 2014, based on a complaint filed by Canon Inc. of Tokyo; Canon U.S.A., Inc. of Melville, New York; and Canon Virginia, Inc. of Newport News, Virginia (collectively, “Canon Complainants”).  See 79 Fed. Reg. 33777 (June 12, 2014).  The Canon Complainants alleged violations by thirty-three respondents of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1337, based upon the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain toner cartridges and components thereof by reason of infringement of certain claims of U.S. Patent No. 8,280,278 (‘‘the ’278 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,630,564 (‘‘the ’564 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,682,215 (‘‘the ’215 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,676,090 (‘‘the ’090 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,369,744 (‘‘the ’744 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,565,640 (‘‘the ’640 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,676,085 (‘‘the ’085 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,135,304 (‘‘the ’304 patent’’); and U.S. Patent No. 8,688,008 (‘‘the ’008 patent’’).  Id. Subsequently, the investigation was partially terminated based on withdrawal of the complaint as to all asserted claims of the following patents: (1) the ‘744 patent; (2) the ‘640 patent; (3) the ‘085 patent; and (4) the ‘304 patent.  See Notice of a Commission Determination Not To Review an Initial Determination Terminating the Investigation as To U.S. Patent Nos. 8,369,744; 8,565,640; 8,676,085; and 8,135,304, Doc. ID 541874 (Sept. 11, 2014).On May 12, 2015, the Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) issued an Initial Determination (“ID”), granting the Canon Complainants’ motion for summary determination of violation and recommending the issuance of a general exclusion order.   See ID at 80 – 249, Doc. ID 556964 (May 12, 2015).    On August 31, 2015, the Commission determined to affirm the ALJ’s finding of a violation of section 337, and issued a general exclusion order (“GEO”) barring entry of certain toner cartridges and components thereof that infringe one or more of claims 160, 165, and 166 of the ’278 patent; claims 171, 176, 179, 181, 189, 192, and 200 of the ’564 patent; claims 23, 26, 27, and 29 of the ’215 patent; claims 1–4 of the ’090 patent; and claims 1, 7–9, 11, 12, and 34 of the ’008 patent.  See 80 Fed. Reg. 53567, 53568 (Sept. 4, 2015).2. The Article at Issue and Arguments Presented to CBPThe article at issue in the 505 Ruling Request (Figures 6 – 10, below) is the 505 Series toner cartridge.  See 505 Ruling Request (“RR”) at 11-15.  Topjet provided CBP with a sample of the 505 toner cartridge for examination.Topjet asserts that the 505 toner cartridge does not infringe any of the patents listed in the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation because the toner cartridge lacks (i) an inclining coupling member that is a required claim element of certain independent claims at issue and (ii) a particular flange design required by the remaining independent claim at issue.   Id. at 21-23. First, Topjet states that the 505 toner cartridge does not possess an inclining coupling member on a separate axis from the developer roller.  See RR at 12-14 and 21.  Rather, the coupling member is set along the same axis as the drum roller and is perpendicular to the drum-end flange (Figures 7-9 below).  Furthermore, the coupling member of the 505 toner cartridge employs a spring system to engage the drive shaft that moves the coupling when compressed horizontally along the longitudinal axis of the photosensitive drum or an axis parallel to the longitudinal axis of the developer roller.  Id. Second, Topjet asserts that the flange on the drum units do not have projections that project radially inward to a greater extent at a position farther from the drum cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder (Figure 10 below). Id. at 15 and 22-23.  Figure 6: Diagram of 505 Cartridge(See RR at 12, Fig. 1B)Figure 7: Diagram of 505 Cartridge Coupling(See RR at 13, Fig. 2B)Figure 8: Cross section of 505 Coupling and Flange (See RR at 13, Fig. 3B)Figure 9: Diagram of 505 Cartridge Coupling Engaged to Drive Shaft(See RR at 14, Fig. 4C)Figure 10:  Cross Section View of 505 Flange(See RR at 15, Fig. 5A)Topjet also cited CBP Rulings HQ H280845 (dated Feb. 1, 2017), HQ H272714 (dated July 1, 2016), and HQ H278406 (dated Mar. 6, 2017) in support of its arguments.  See RR at 15-16.  Topjet argued that its 505 toner cartridge is substantially similar to the products in question in these three rulings and accordingly, Topjet concluded that, similar to the holdings in these rulings, the 505 toner cartridge is outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation. Id. An examination by CBP of the diagrams and schematics, Figures 7-11 above, of the 505 toner cartridge coupling and drum flange revealed that the coupling does not pivot, moves only coaxial to the drum unit, and that it is set perpendicular to the flange of the drum unit.  Lastly, an examination of the cross-sectioned drum flange diagrams for the 505 cartridge, Figure 10 above, reveals that its projections do not project radially inward to a greater extent at a position farther from the drum cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder.  Rather, the projections appear to project radially inward the same uniform distance throughout the drum flange, regardless of position relative to the drum cylinder.ISSUE:Whether the 505 toner cartridge infringes any of claims 160, 165, and 166 of the ’278 patent; claims 171, 176, 179, 181, 189, 192, and 200 of the ’564 patent; claims 23, 26, 27, and 29 of the ’215 patent; claims 1–4 of the ’090 patent; and claims 1, 7–9, 11, 12, and 34 of the ’008 patent, and are therefore within the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.LAW AND ANALYSIS:Law of Patent InfringementUnder section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. § 1337, the Commission has authority to conduct investigations into imported articles that allegedly infringe United States patents and impose remedies if the accused articles are found to be infringing. See 19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(1)(B), (b)(1), (d), (f), (i). 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d), in particular, empowers the Commission to direct the exclusion from entry of articles found to infringe the asserted patents. When the Commission determines there is infringement and thus a violation of section 337, it generally issues one of two types of exclusion orders: (1) a limited exclusion order or (2) a general exclusion order. See Fuji Photo Film Co., Ltd. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 474 F.3d 1281, 1286 (Fed. Cir. 2007).Both types of orders direct CBP to bar infringing products from entering the country. See Yingbin-Nature (Guangdong) Wood Indus. Co. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 535 F.3d 1322, 1330 (Fed Cir. 2008). “A limited exclusion order is ‘limited’ in that it only applies to the specific parties before the Commission in the investigation. In contrast, a general exclusion order bars the importation of infringing products by everyone, regardless of whether they were respondents in the Commission's investigation.” Id. A general exclusion order is appropriate only if two exceptional circumstances apply. See Kyocera Wireless Corp. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 545 F.3d 1340, 1356. A general exclusion order may only be issued if (1) “necessary to prevent circumvention of a limited exclusion order,” or (2) “there is a pattern of violation of this section and it is difficult to identify the source of infringing products.” 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)(2); see Kyocera, 545 F.3d at 1356 (“If a complainant wishes to obtain an exclusion order operative against articles of non-respondents, it must seek a GEO [general exclusion order] by satisfying the heightened burdens of §§ 1337(d)(2)(A) and (B).”).In addition to the action taken above, the Commission may issue an order under 19 U.S.C. § 1337(i) directing CBP to seize and forfeit articles attempting entry in violation of an exclusion order if their owner, importer, or consignee previously had articles denied entry on the basis of that exclusion order and received notice that seizure and forfeiture would result from any future attempt to enter articles subject to the same. An exclusion order under § 1337(d)—either limited or general—and a seizure and forfeiture order under § 1337(i) apply at the border only and are operative against articles presented for customs examination or articles conditionally released from customs custody but still subject to a timely demand for redelivery. See 19 U.S.C. §§ 1337(d)(1) (“The Commission shall notify the Secretary of the Treasury of its action under this subsection directing such exclusion from entry, and upon receipt of such notice, the Secretary shall, through the proper officers, refuse such entry.”); id. at (i)(3) (“Upon the attempted entry of articles subject to an order issued under this subsection, the Secretary of the Treasury shall immediately notify all ports of entry of the attempted importation and shall identify the persons notified under paragraph (1)(C).”) (emphasis added); see also ClearCorrect Operating, LLC v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 810 F.3d 1283, 1295 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (“This section [1337(i)] permits the Commission to exclude ‘articles’ from importation into the United States; however, it is difficult to see how one could physically stop electronic transmissions at the borders under the current statutory scheme…. A construction of the term ‘articles’ that includes electronically transmitted digital data is also not reasonable when applied to Section 337(i)(3). This section reads, ‘[u]pon the attempted entry of articles subject to an order issued under this subsection, the Secretary of the Treasury shall immediately notify all ports of entry of the attempted importation and shall identify the persons notified under paragraph (1)(C).’ Not only can an electronic transmission not be subject to an ‘attempted entry’ through a ‘port of entry,’ it also cannot be intercepted at a ‘port of entry’ as contemplated in the statute.”) (emphasis added), reh’ng en banc denied by Clearcorrect Operating v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 819 F.3d 1334 (Fed. Cir. 2016).Significantly, unlike district court injunctions, the Commission can issue a general exclusion order that broadly prohibits entry of articles that infringe the relevant claims of an asserted patent without regard to whether the persons importing such articles were parties to, or were related to parties to, the investigation that led to issuance of the general exclusion order. See Vastfame Camera, Ltd. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 386 F.3d 1108, 1114 (Fed. Cir. 2004). The Commission also has recognized that even limited exclusion orders have broader applicability beyond just the parties found to infringe during an investigation. See Certain GPS Devices and Products Containing Same, Inv. No. 337-TA-602, Comm’n Op. at 17, n. 6, Doc ID 317981 (Jan. 2009) (“We do not view the Court’s opinion in Kyocera as affecting the issuance of LEOs [limited exclusion orders] that exclude infringing products made by respondents found to be violating Section 337, but imported by another entity. For example, the traditional test for injunctive relief, used by district courts in accordance with the Supreme Court’s eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C., 547 U.S. 388 (2006), opinion “does not apply to Commission remedy determinations under Section 337.” Spansion, Inc. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 629 F.3d 1331, 1359 (Fed. Cir. 2010). Reels of Super 8mm Film, 413 U.S. 123 (1973) (“Import restrictions and searches of persons or packages at the national borders rest on different considerations and different rules of constitutional law from domestic regulations. Stranahan, 192 U.S. 470 (1904) (“As a result of the complete power of Congress over foreign commerce, it necessarily follows that no individual has a vested right to trade with foreign nations, which is so broad in character as to limit and restrict the power of Congress to determine what articles of merchandise may be imported into this country and the terms upon which a right to import may be exercised. All of the independent claims at issue of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents recite a coupling member that is movable between a first position in which the coupling member is substantially parallel to (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) or coaxial with (claim 160 of the ’278 patent, claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and claim 23 of the ’215 patent) an axis of a rotary member (claim 160 of the ’278 patent) / photosensitive drum (claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and  claim 23 of the ’215 patent) / developing roller (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) and a second position in which the coupling member is inclined with respect to the axis of the rotary member / photosensitive drum / developing roller.  As such, these independent claims require an inclining moveable coupling member that, prior to when a toner cartridge is inserted into a printer, the coupling member inclines on an axis separate from the axis of the drum unit.  When the toner cartridge is fully engaged in the printer, the moveable coupling member pivots to become coaxial with the drum unit.  Figure 1 on page 9 above demonstrates an example of the type of moveable coupling member that infringes the claims of the patents. As noted supra, Topjet asserts that its 505 cartridge does not infringe these patents because its toner cartridge does not possess the inclining, moveable coupling member as recited in the relevant patent claims.  According to Topjet, the 505 cartridge employs a coupling member that moves only perpendicular to the same axis as the drum unit.  An examination by CBP of the picture and schematic of the 505 cartridge in Figures 7-9 (page 11 above) confirms Topjet’s assertion.  The coupling members depicted in Figures 7-9 use a spring system that allows the coupling to move horizontally back and forth when compressed so that it engages the drive shaft of the printer to rotate the photosensitive drum when in use.  Because the 505 cartridge does not possess a coupling member that is moveable between first and second positions in the manner recited in the relevant claims, this toner cartridge does not meet all the claim elements of any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, or ’008 patents, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Topjet’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).“Angle of Inclination of Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsIn addition to the claim element that requires that a toner cartridge possess a moveable coupling member as described above, such a coupling member’s axis must also pivot within a 20 degree to 60-degree range from the axis of the drum unit.  This claim element is found in the following claims:  claim 160 of the ’278 patent; claim 171 of the ’564 patent; claim 23 of the ’215 patent, and claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent.As described above, the couplings on the 505 cartridge does not pivot at all.  Rather, the coupling on this toner cartridge moves coaxial only with the axis of the drum unit.  Because the coupling does not pivot at all, it does not create any angle of inclination that falls within 20 degrees to 60 degrees (or any degrees) from that of the drum unit’s axis and thus does not meet the claim elements of the asserted claims listed in the preceding paragraph of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents that have an angle of inclination requirement.  Canon does not dispute Topjet’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).The ’090 PatentIndependent claim 1 of the ’090 patent recites an electrophotographic photosensitive drum unit that includes a cylinder and a drum flange provided at one end of the cylinder.  The drum flange includes at least two projections that are provided inside of the drum flange and that project radially inwardly of the drum flange.  Claim 1 further recites, in relevant part that “each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.”An examination of Topjet’s drum flange for the 505 cartridge in Figure 10 (page 12 above) reveals that the projections in the flange extend radially inward to the same extent along their entire length from a position close to the drum to a position farthest from the drum.  Thus, these projections inside this flange does not extend radially inward to a greater extent at a position further away from the drum cylinder.  As such, the 505 toner cartridge does not meet all the elements of claim 1 of the ’090 patent, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Topjet’s arguments regarding the ‘090 patent as to this basis for non-infringement.  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).Therefore, based on the evidence in the record, we find that Topjet has met its burden to show that the 505 toner cartridge does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.   Thus, the 505 toner cartridge is outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.  HOLDING:The 505 toner cartridge manufactured by Topjet Technology Co., Ltd., does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.  As such, the 505 toner cartridge is not subject to exclusion from entry for consumption into the United States, entry for consumption from a foreign-trade zone, or withdrawal from a warehouse for consumption.This decision is limited to the facts set forth herein.  If Topjet manufactures or imports toner cartridges and drum units whose designs differs from the embodiment described above, or if future importations vary from the facts stipulated to herein, this decision shall not be binding on CBP as provided for in 19 C.F.R. §§177.2(b)(1), (2), and (4), and §§ 177.9(b)(1) and (2).					Sincerely,					Charles R. If these independent claims are not infringed, then none of the dependent claims in these patents are infringed.  “It is axiomatic that dependent claims cannot be found infringed unless the claims from which they depend have been found to have been infringed[.]”  Wahpeton Canvas Co. v. Frontier, Inc., 870 F.2d 1546, 1553 (Fed. Cir. 1989); See also Becton, 922 F.2d, at 798.  Thus, the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation applies to articles manufactured or imported by Topjet only if they infringe any of the listed claims above for any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, and ’090 patents.Infringement AnalysisThere are two different claim elements of patents ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 at issue with the 505 toner cartridge: (1) an inclining moveable coupling member and (2) the angle of inclination of the moveable coupling member.  These claim elements are addressed in turn.“Inclining Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsTo infringe on any of the independent claims at issue of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents, a toner cartridge must possess a coupling member that meets the claim language highlighted in bold, above, in section I(B)(2).  All of the independent claims at issue of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents recite a coupling member that is movable between a first position in which the coupling member is substantially parallel to (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) or coaxial with (claim 160 of the ’278 patent, claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and claim 23 of the ’215 patent) an axis of a rotary member (claim 160 of the ’278 patent) / photosensitive drum (claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and  claim 23 of the ’215 patent) / developing roller (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) and a second position in which the coupling member is inclined with respect to the axis of the rotary member / photosensitive drum / developing roller.  As such, these independent claims require an inclining moveable coupling member that, prior to when a toner cartridge is inserted into a printer, the coupling member inclines on an axis separate from the axis of the drum unit.  When the toner cartridge is fully engaged in the printer, the moveable coupling member pivots to become coaxial with the drum unit.  Figure 1 on page 9 above demonstrates an example of the type of moveable coupling member that infringes the claims of the patents. As noted supra, Topjet asserts that its 505 cartridge does not infringe these patents because its toner cartridge does not possess the inclining, moveable coupling member as recited in the relevant patent claims.  According to Topjet, the 505 cartridge employs a coupling member that moves only perpendicular to the same axis as the drum unit.  An examination by CBP of the picture and schematic of the 505 cartridge in Figures 7-9 (page 11 above) confirms Topjet’s assertion.  The coupling members depicted in Figures 7-9 use a spring system that allows the coupling to move horizontally back and forth when compressed so that it engages the drive shaft of the printer to rotate the photosensitive drum when in use.  Because the 505 cartridge does not possess a coupling member that is moveable between first and second positions in the manner recited in the relevant claims, this toner cartridge does not meet all the claim elements of any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, or ’008 patents, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Topjet’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).“Angle of Inclination of Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsIn addition to the claim element that requires that a toner cartridge possess a moveable coupling member as described above, such a coupling member’s axis must also pivot within a 20 degree to 60-degree range from the axis of the drum unit.  This claim element is found in the following claims:  claim 160 of the ’278 patent; claim 171 of the ’564 patent; claim 23 of the ’215 patent, and claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent.As described above, the couplings on the 505 cartridge does not pivot at all.  Rather, the coupling on this toner cartridge moves coaxial only with the axis of the drum unit.  Because the coupling does not pivot at all, it does not create any angle of inclination that falls within 20 degrees to 60 degrees (or any degrees) from that of the drum unit’s axis and thus does not meet the claim elements of the asserted claims listed in the preceding paragraph of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents that have an angle of inclination requirement.  Canon does not dispute Topjet’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).The ’090 PatentIndependent claim 1 of the ’090 patent recites an electrophotographic photosensitive drum unit that includes a cylinder and a drum flange provided at one end of the cylinder.  The drum flange includes at least two projections that are provided inside of the drum flange and that project radially inwardly of the drum flange.  Claim 1 further recites, in relevant part that “each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.”An examination of Topjet’s drum flange for the 505 cartridge in Figure 10 (page 12 above) reveals that the projections in the flange extend radially inward to the same extent along their entire length from a position close to the drum to a position farthest from the drum.  Thus, these projections inside this flange does not extend radially inward to a greater extent at a position further away from the drum cylinder.  As such, the 505 toner cartridge does not meet all the elements of claim 1 of the ’090 patent, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Topjet’s arguments regarding the ‘090 patent as to this basis for non-infringement.  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).Therefore, based on the evidence in the record, we find that Topjet has met its burden to show that the 505 toner cartridge does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.   Thus, the 505 toner cartridge is outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.
sections.HOLDING: The 505 toner cartridge manufactured by Topjet Technology Co., Ltd., does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.  As such, the 505 toner cartridge is not subject to exclusion from entry for consumption into the United States, entry for consumption from a foreign-trade zone, or withdrawal from a warehouse for consumption.This decision is limited to the facts set forth herein.  If Topjet manufactures or imports toner cartridges and drum units whose designs differs from the embodiment described above, or if future importations vary from the facts stipulated to herein, this decision shall not be binding on CBP as provided for in 19 C.F.R. §§177.2(b)(1), (2), and (4), and §§ 177.9(b)(1) and (2).					Sincerely,					Charles R. Steuart, Chief					Intellectual Property Rights Branch

The Article at Issue and Arguments Presented to CBPThe article at issue in the Ruling Request (Figures 6 – 11, below) is the ZFI toner cartridge.  See Ruling Request, pp. 1-2 (Dec. 20, 2017).   Zhuhai Fast Image provided CBP with a sample of the ZFI toner cartridge, labeled as compatible with a CF226A Hewlett Packard printer, for examination.  Zhuhai Fast Image noted in its ruling request that this cartridge model is representative of all its toner cartridges that utilize the FAST drum flange and coupling member described herein and listed in the ruling request appendix.  Id. at 11, n. 3; Appendix A.Zhuhai Fast Image asserts that the ZFI toner cartridge does not infringe any of the patents listed in the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation because it lacks (i) an inclining coupling member that is a required claim element of certain independent claims at issue and (ii) a particular flange design required by the remaining independent claim at issue.   Id. at 15-19.First, Zhuhai Fast Image states that the ZFI toner cartridge does not possess an inclining coupling member on a separate axis from the developer roller.  See Ruling Request at 16-17, Figures 13-15.   Rather, the coupling member is stationary along the same axis as the drum roller and is perpendicular to the drum-end flange (Figures 8 and 9 below).Second, Zhuhai Fast Image asserts that the flange on the drum units of the ZFI toner cartridge do not have projections that project radially inward to a greater extent at a position farther from the drum cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder. Id. at 17.  Zhuhai Fast Image stated that the radial protections inside its drum flange, Figures 10 and 11 below, “project radially inward to the same extent regardless of whether the position is farther from, or closer to, the cylinder.”  Id. at 17-18, Figures 16-18.Figure 6: Picture of the Submitted ZFI Toner CartridgeFigure 7: ZFI Toner Cartridge Side View(See RR at 12, Fig 8)Figure 8: Zhuhai Fast Image Flange with Coupling(See RR at 14, Fig 12)Figure 9: Submitted Samples of CouplingsFigure 10:  Cross Section View of Submitted Drum FlangeFigure 11: Cross Section of Zhuhai Fast Image Flange(See RR at 18, Fig. 17)Zhuhai Fast Image also cited CBP Ruling HQ H280845 (dated Feb. 1, 2017) in support of its arguments.    Zhuhai Fast Image argued that the ZFI toner cartridge is substantially similar to the products in question in H280845 and accordingly, Zhuhai Fast Image concluded that, similar to the holding in H280845, the ZFI toner cartridge is outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.  See Ruling Request, p 2. An examination by CBP of the sample ZFI toner cartridge and drum flanges revealed that the coupling does not pivot or move at all and that it is set perpendicular to the flange of the drum unit.  An examination of the cross sectioned drum flange reveals that its projections do not project radially inward to a greater extent at a position farther from the drum cylinder that at a position closer to the cylinder.  Rather, the projections appear to project radially inward the same uniform distance throughout the drum flange, regardless of position relative to the drum cylinder.ISSUE:Whether the ZFI toner cartridge infringes any of claims 160, 165, and 166 of the ’278 patent; claims 171, 176, 179, 181, 189, 192, and 200 of the ’564 patent; claims 23, 26, 27, and 29 of the ’215 patent; claims 1–4 of the ’090 patent; and claims 1, 7–9, 11, 12, and 34 of the ’008 patent, and is therefore within the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.LAW AND ANALYSIS:Law of Patent InfringementUnder section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. § 1337, the Commission has authority to conduct investigations into imported articles that allegedly infringe United States patents and impose remedies if the accused articles are found to be infringing. See 19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(1)(B), (b)(1), (d), (f), (i). 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d), in particular, empowers the Commission to direct the exclusion from entry of articles found to infringe the asserted patents. When the Commission determines there is infringement and thus a violation of section 337, it generally issues one of two types of exclusion orders: (1) a limited exclusion order or (2) a general exclusion order. See Fuji Photo Film Co., Ltd. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 474 F.3d 1281, 1286 (Fed. Cir. 2007).Both types of orders direct CBP to bar infringing products from entering the country. See Yingbin-Nature (Guangdong) Wood Indus. Co. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 535 F.3d 1322, 1330 (Fed Cir. 2008). “A limited exclusion order is ‘limited’ in that it only applies to the specific parties before the Commission in the investigation. In contrast, a general exclusion order bars the importation of infringing products by everyone, regardless of whether they were respondents in the Commission's investigation.” Id. A general exclusion order is appropriate only if two exceptional circumstances apply. See Kyocera Wireless Corp. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 545 F.3d 1340, 1356. A general exclusion order may only be issued if (1) “necessary to prevent circumvention of a limited exclusion order,” or (2) “there is a pattern of violation of this section and it is difficult to identify the source of infringing products.” 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)(2); see Kyocera, 545 F.3d at 1356 (“If a complainant wishes to obtain an exclusion order operative against articles of non-respondents, it must seek a GEO [general exclusion order] by satisfying the heightened burdens of §§ 1337(d)(2)(A) and (B).”).In addition to the action taken above, the Commission may issue an order under 19 U.S.C. § 1337(i) directing CBP to seize and forfeit articles attempting entry in violation of an exclusion order if their owner, importer, or consignee previously had articles denied entry on the basis of that exclusion order and received notice that seizure and forfeiture would result from any future attempt to enter articles subject to the same. An exclusion order under § 1337(d)—either limited or general—and a seizure and forfeiture order under § 1337(i) apply at the border only and are operative against articles presented for customs examination or articles conditionally released from customs custody but still subject to a timely demand for redelivery. See 19 U.S.C. §§ 1337(d)(1) (“The Commission shall notify the Secretary of the Treasury of its action under this subsection directing such exclusion from entry, and upon receipt of such notice, the Secretary shall, through the proper officers, refuse such entry.”); id. at (i)(3) (“Upon the attempted entry of articles subject to an order issued under this subsection, the Secretary of the Treasury shall immediately notify all ports of entry of the attempted importation and shall identify the persons notified under paragraph (1)(C).”) (emphasis added); see also ClearCorrect Operating, LLC v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 810 F.3d 1283, 1295 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (“This section [1337(i)] permits the Commission to exclude ‘articles’ from importation into the United States; however, it is difficult to see how one could physically stop electronic transmissions at the borders under the current statutory scheme…. A construction of the term ‘articles’ that includes electronically transmitted digital data is also not reasonable when applied to Section 337(i)(3). This section reads, ‘[u]pon the attempted entry of articles subject to an order issued under this subsection, the Secretary of the Treasury shall immediately notify all ports of entry of the attempted importation and shall identify the persons notified under paragraph (1)(C).’ Not only can an electronic transmission not be subject to an ‘attempted entry’ through a ‘port of entry,’ it also cannot be intercepted at a ‘port of entry’ as contemplated in the statute.”) (emphasis added), reh’ng en banc denied by Clearcorrect Operating v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 819 F.3d 1334 (Fed. Cir. 2016).Significantly, unlike district court injunctions, the Commission can issue a general exclusion order that broadly prohibits entry of articles that infringe the relevant claims of an asserted patent without regard to whether the persons importing such articles were parties to, or were related to parties to, the investigation that led to issuance of the general exclusion order. See Vastfame Camera, Ltd. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 386 F.3d 1108, 1114 (Fed. Cir. 2004). The Commission also has recognized that even limited exclusion orders have broader applicability beyond just the parties found to infringe during an investigation. See Certain GPS Devices and Products Containing Same, Inv. No. 337-TA-602, Comm’n Op. at 17, n. 6, Doc ID 317981 (Jan. 2009) (“We do not view the Court’s opinion in Kyocera as affecting the issuance of LEOs [limited exclusion orders] that exclude infringing products made by respondents found to be violating Section 337, but imported by another entity. The exclusionary language in this regard that is traditionally included in LEOs is consistent with 19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(1)(B)–(D) and 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)(1).”).However, this is not the only difference between district court injunctions under section 283 of the Patent Act and Commission exclusion orders under section 337 of the Tariff Act. For example, the traditional test for injunctive relief, used by district courts in accordance with the Supreme Court’s eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C., 547 U.S. 388 (2006), opinion “does not apply to Commission remedy determinations under Section 337.” Spansion, Inc. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 629 F.3d 1331, 1359 (Fed. Cir. 2010). This difference between exclusion orders under Section 337 and injunctions under the Patent Act follows “the long-standing principle that importation is treated differently than domestic activity.” Id. at 1360 (citing United States v. 12 200-Ft. Reels of Super 8mm Film, 413 U.S. 123 (1973) (“Import restrictions and searches of persons or packages at the national borders rest on different considerations and different rules of constitutional law from domestic regulations. The Constitution gives Congress broad, comprehensive powers ‘to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations.’ Art. I, § 8, cl. 3.”); see Buttfield v. Stranahan, 192 U.S. 470 (1904) (“As a result of the complete power of Congress over foreign commerce, it necessarily follows that no individual has a vested right to trade with foreign nations, which is so broad in character as to limit and restrict the power of Congress to determine what articles of merchandise may be imported into this country and the terms upon which a right to import may be exercised. TiVo Inc. v. Echostar Corp., 646 F.3d 869, 876 (Fed. Cir. 2011) (en banc). Under this test, if new or redesigned products are so different from the product previously found  to infringe (focusing not on differences randomly chosen between the two but on the specific features of the product found to infringe in the earlier infringement trial), such that they raise a fair ground of doubt as to the wrongfulness of the defendant's conduct, the new or redesigned products are deemed to be more than colorably different from the legacy one adjudged to be infringing and violation of the injunction at this point would not be the appropriate consideration. Instead, a new trial would be required to litigate the infringement question. Id. at 881-83. The initial inquiry under the colorable differences test, therefore, focuses on whether the modification in question is significant. Id.Exclusion orders, however, apply to any articles—new, modified, or otherwise— that are “covered by” the patent claims included in the exclusion order. See Certain Optical Disk Controller Chips and Chipsets, Inv. No. 337-TA-506, Comm’n Op. at 56-57, USITC Pub. 3935, Doc ID 287263 (July 2007) (“The Commission's long-standing practice is to direct its remedial orders to all products covered by the patent claims as to which a violation has been found, rather than limiting its orders only to those specific models selected for the infringement analysis...[W]hile individual models may be evaluated to determine importation and infringement, the Commission's jurisdiction extends to all models of infringing products that are imported at the time of the Commission's determination and to all such products that will be imported during the life of the remedial orders.”). U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 645 F.2d 976, 988–89 (C.C.P.A. 1981)).This approach is supported by Federal Circuit precedent. See Hyundai Elecs. Indus. Co. v. U.S. Int'l Trade Comm'n, 899 F.2d 1204, 1210 (Fed. Cir. 1990) (“Indeed, we have recognized, and Hyundai does not dispute, that in an appropriate case the Commission can impose a general exclusion order that binds parties and non-parties alike and effectively shifts to would-be importers of potentially infringing articles, as a condition of entry, the burden of establishing noninfringement. Frontier, Inc., 870 F.2d 1546, 1553 (Fed. Cir. 1989); See also Becton, 922 F.2d, at 798. These claim elements are addressed in turn.“Inclining Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsTo infringe on any of the independent claims at issue of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents, a toner cartridge must possess a coupling member that meets the claim language highlighted in bold, above, in section I(B)(2).  All of the independent claims at issue of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents recite a coupling member that is movable between a first position in which the coupling member is substantially parallel to (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) or coaxial with (claim 160 of the ’278 patent, claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and claim 23 of the ’215 patent) an axis of a rotary member (claim 160 of the ’278 patent) / photosensitive drum (claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and  claim 23 of the ’215 patent) / developing roller (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) and a second position in which the coupling member is inclined with respect to the axis of the rotary member / photosensitive drum / developing roller.  As such, these independent claims require an inclining moveable coupling member that, prior to when a toner cartridge is inserted into a printer, the coupling member inclines on an axis separate from the axis of the drum unit.  When the toner cartridge is fully engaged in the printer, the moveable coupling member pivots to become coaxial with the drum unit.  Figure 1 on page 7 above demonstrates what type of moveable coupling member infringes the claims of the patents. As noted supra, Zhuhai Fast Image asserts that the ZFI toner cartridge does not infringe these patents because its article does not possess the inclining, moveable coupling member as recited in the relevant patent claims.  According to Zhuhai Fast Image, the ZFI toner cartridge has a coupling member that does not move in its own plane or perpendicular to the same axis as the drum unit, but is firmly set in the flange.  An examination by CBP of a sample of the ZFI toner cartridge, as depicted in Figures 7 and 8 (page 10 above), confirms Zhuhai Fast Image’s assertion.  The coupling member in Figures 7, 8, and 9 (page 10 above) is coupled with the drive shaft of the printer when the cartridge is inserted into the printer.  Because the ZFI toner cartridge does not possess a coupling member that is moveable between first and second positions in the manner recited in the relevant claims, these articles do not meet all the claim elements of any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, or ’008 patents, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Fast Image’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.“Angle of Inclination of Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsIn addition to the claim element that requires that a toner cartridge possess a moveable coupling member as described above, such a coupling member’s axis must also pivot within a 20 degree to 60-degree range from the axis of the drum unit.  This claim element is found in the following claims:  claim 160 of the ’278 patent; claim 171 of the ’564 patent; claim 23 of the ’215 patent, and claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent.As described above, the coupling member on the ZFI toner cartridge does not pivot at all.  Rather, the coupling on the ZFI toner cartridge is set in place in the flange coaxial with the axis of the drum unit.  Because the coupling does not pivot at all it does not create any angle of inclination that falls within 20 degrees to 60 degrees (or any degrees) from that of the drum unit’s axis and thus does not meet the claim elements of the asserted claims listed in the preceding paragraph of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents that have an angle of inclination requirement.  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Fast Image’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.The ’090 PatentIndependent claim 1 of the ’090 patent recites an electrophotographic photosensitive drum unit that includes a cylinder and a drum flange provided at one end of the cylinder.  The drum flange includes at least two projections that are provided inside of the drum flange and that project radially inwardly of the drum flange.  Claim 1 further recites, in relevant part that “each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.”An examination of Zhuhai Fast Image’s FAST drum flange in Figures 10 and 11 (page 10 above) reveals that the projections in the flange extend radially inward to the same extent along their entire length from a position close to the drum to a position farthest from the drum.  Thus, these projections inside the flange do not extend radially inward to a greater extent at a position further away from the drum cylinder.  As such, the ZFI toner cartridge does not meet all the elements of claim 1 of the ’090 patent, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Fast Image’s arguments regarding the ‘090 patent as to this basis for non-infringement.Therefore, based on the evidence in the record, we find that Zhuhai Fast Image has met its burden to show that the ZFI toner cartridge does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.  Thus, the ZFI toner cartridge is outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.  HOLDING:The ZFI toner cartridge manufactured by Zhuhai Fast Image Products Co., Ltd. does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.  As such, ZFI toner cartridges are not subject to exclusion from entry for consumption into the United States, entry for consumption from a foreign-trade zone, or withdrawal from a warehouse for consumption.This decision is limited to the facts set forth herein.  If Zhuhai Fast Image manufactures or imports toner cartridges and drum units whose designs differs from the embodiment described above, or if future importations vary from the facts stipulated to herein, this decision shall not be binding on CBP as provided for in 19 C.F.R. §§177.2(b)(1), (2), and (4), and §§ 177.9(b)(1) and (2).					Sincerely,					Charles R. Thus, the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation applies to articles manufactured or imported by Zhuhai Fast Image only if they infringe any of the listed claims above for any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, and ’090 patents.Infringement AnalysisThere are two different claim elements of patents ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 at issue with the ZFI toner cartridge: (1) an inclining moveable coupling member and (2) the angle of inclination of the moveable coupling member.  These claim elements are addressed in turn.“Inclining Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsTo infringe on any of the independent claims at issue of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents, a toner cartridge must possess a coupling member that meets the claim language highlighted in bold, above, in section I(B)(2).  All of the independent claims at issue of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents recite a coupling member that is movable between a first position in which the coupling member is substantially parallel to (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) or coaxial with (claim 160 of the ’278 patent, claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and claim 23 of the ’215 patent) an axis of a rotary member (claim 160 of the ’278 patent) / photosensitive drum (claims 171, 179, 189, and 200 of the ’564 patent, and  claim 23 of the ’215 patent) / developing roller (claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent) and a second position in which the coupling member is inclined with respect to the axis of the rotary member / photosensitive drum / developing roller.  As such, these independent claims require an inclining moveable coupling member that, prior to when a toner cartridge is inserted into a printer, the coupling member inclines on an axis separate from the axis of the drum unit.  When the toner cartridge is fully engaged in the printer, the moveable coupling member pivots to become coaxial with the drum unit.  Figure 1 on page 7 above demonstrates what type of moveable coupling member infringes the claims of the patents. As noted supra, Zhuhai Fast Image asserts that the ZFI toner cartridge does not infringe these patents because its article does not possess the inclining, moveable coupling member as recited in the relevant patent claims.  According to Zhuhai Fast Image, the ZFI toner cartridge has a coupling member that does not move in its own plane or perpendicular to the same axis as the drum unit, but is firmly set in the flange.  An examination by CBP of a sample of the ZFI toner cartridge, as depicted in Figures 7 and 8 (page 10 above), confirms Zhuhai Fast Image’s assertion.  The coupling member in Figures 7, 8, and 9 (page 10 above) is coupled with the drive shaft of the printer when the cartridge is inserted into the printer.  Because the ZFI toner cartridge does not possess a coupling member that is moveable between first and second positions in the manner recited in the relevant claims, these articles do not meet all the claim elements of any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, or ’008 patents, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Fast Image’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.“Angle of Inclination of Moveable Coupling Member” Claim Element of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 PatentsIn addition to the claim element that requires that a toner cartridge possess a moveable coupling member as described above, such a coupling member’s axis must also pivot within a 20 degree to 60-degree range from the axis of the drum unit.  This claim element is found in the following claims:  claim 160 of the ’278 patent; claim 171 of the ’564 patent; claim 23 of the ’215 patent, and claims 1 and 12 of the ’008 patent.As described above, the coupling member on the ZFI toner cartridge does not pivot at all.  Rather, the coupling on the ZFI toner cartridge is set in place in the flange coaxial with the axis of the drum unit.  Because the coupling does not pivot at all it does not create any angle of inclination that falls within 20 degrees to 60 degrees (or any degrees) from that of the drum unit’s axis and thus does not meet the claim elements of the asserted claims listed in the preceding paragraph of the ’278, ’564, ’215, and ’008 patents that have an angle of inclination requirement.  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Fast Image’s arguments as to this basis for non-infringement.The ’090 PatentIndependent claim 1 of the ’090 patent recites an electrophotographic photosensitive drum unit that includes a cylinder and a drum flange provided at one end of the cylinder.  The drum flange includes at least two projections that are provided inside of the drum flange and that project radially inwardly of the drum flange.  Claim 1 further recites, in relevant part that “each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.”An examination of Zhuhai Fast Image’s FAST drum flange in Figures 10 and 11 (page 10 above) reveals that the projections in the flange extend radially inward to the same extent along their entire length from a position close to the drum to a position farthest from the drum.  Thus, these projections inside the flange do not extend radially inward to a greater extent at a position further away from the drum cylinder.  As such, the ZFI toner cartridge does not meet all the elements of claim 1 of the ’090 patent, or any of the claims that depend therefrom.  Canon does not dispute Zhuhai Fast Image’s arguments regarding the ‘090 patent as to this basis for non-infringement.Therefore, based on the evidence in the record, we find that Zhuhai Fast Image has met its burden to show that the ZFI toner cartridge does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.  Thus, the ZFI toner cartridge is outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.
sections.HOLDING: The ZFI toner cartridge manufactured by Zhuhai Fast Image Products Co., Ltd. does not infringe any of the independent claims at issue of any of the ’278, ’564, ’215, ’008, or ’090 patents, or any of the claims at issue that depend therefrom.  As such, ZFI toner cartridges are not subject to exclusion from entry for consumption into the United States, entry for consumption from a foreign-trade zone, or withdrawal from a warehouse for consumption.This decision is limited to the facts set forth herein.  If Zhuhai Fast Image manufactures or imports toner cartridges and drum units whose designs differs from the embodiment described above, or if future importations vary from the facts stipulated to herein, this decision shall not be binding on CBP as provided for in 19 C.F.R. §§177.2(b)(1), (2), and (4), and §§ 177.9(b)(1) and (2).					Sincerely,					Charles R. Steuart, Chief					Intellectual Property Rights Branch

We hold that the toner cartridges at issue in this ruling letter are not subject to the general exclusion order (“GEO”) issued by the U.S. International Trade Commission (“ITC” or “Commission”) in Investigation No. 337-TA-918 (“the ’918 investigation”).  This ruling letter is the result of an inter partes proceeding administered by CBP.  The inter partes proceeding involved the two parties with a direct and demonstrable interest in the question presented by the ruling request: your clients, Topjet Technology Co., Ltd., Maxwell Image Ltd., and E-Z Ink, Inc. (collectively, “Requesters” or “Topjet”) and Canon Inc. of Japan, Canon U.S.A., Inc. of Melville, New York, and Canon Virginia, Inc. of Newport News, Virginia (collectively, “Canon”).BACKGROUND:A. 	Rule 177 Proceeding before the IPR Branch	On December 22, 2017, Requesters submitted a letter (“Ruling Request”) requesting administrative rulings pursuant to 19 C.F.R. part 177 as to whether certain toner cartridges (“the Topjet toner cartridges”) manufactured by Topjet Technology Co., Ltd., imported by E-Z Ink, Inc., and sold by Maxwell Image Ltd. would be subject to the GEO issued by the ITC in the ’918 investigation.  See Ruling Request at 1-2 and 11, Dec. 22, 2017.  Specifically, the Ruling Request seeks a ruling with respect to two types of toner cartridges: HP 217 series compatible cartridges (“217 toner cartridges”) and HP 226 series compatible cartridges (“226 toner cartridges”).  Topjet submitted samples of the 217 toner cartridges and the 226 toner cartridges with the Ruling Request.  On January 19, 2018, Topjet indicated that a copy of the Ruling Request was provided to Canon and requested return of the samples provided to CBP to provide Cannon an opportunity to review the Topjet toner cartridges.  See E-mail from David Farnum, counsel for Topjet, to William Wittwer, attorney-advisor at CBP (Jan. 19, 2018).On February 2, 2018, Canon responded to the Ruling Request, indicating that it reviewed the Topjet toner cartridges, and that it “does not object to the requested rulings that the Topjet cartridges do not fall within the scope of the GEO issued in Investigation No. 337-TA-918, but it disagrees with one aspect of Requesters’ arguments…”  See E-mail from Michael Sandonato, counsel for Canon, to William Wittwer and Edmund Haughey, counsel for Canon (Feb. 2, 2018).  Specifically, Canon stated:The disagreement relates to claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 8,676,090 (“the ’090 patent”).  This claim requires, among other things, a drum flange that includes “at least two projections provided inside of the drum flange and projected radially inwardly of the drum flange, with a space diametrically between the two projections.”  The claim further requires that “each of the two projections projects radially inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than it does at a position closer to the cylinder.”  Requesters assert that the Topjet cartridges do not infringe the claims of the ’090 patent because the cartridges do not have flanges with projections that project radially inward toward the center of the flange.  Canon disagrees, and believes that the flange on each of the subject cartridges includes at least two projections that project radially inward.  Requesters further assert that there are no projections that are “closer together farther from the drum,” i.e., that project radially inwardly to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder.  Canon does not dispute this latter point, and accordingly does not dispute Requesters’ ultimate conclusion with respect to the ’090 patent. Id.  Canon further stated that “[p]rovided that Requesters withdraw their argument with respect to the ’090 patent that the flanges in the Topjet cartridges lack inward projections and/or CBP limits its ruling to the undisputed part of Requesters’ arguments (i.e., that each drum flange does not have projections that project inwardly of the drum flange to a greater extent at a position farther from the cylinder than they do at a position closer to the cylinder), we see no reason for Canon to participate in this proceeding.”  Id. In response to Canon, Topjet agreed to: (i) withdraw its argument that the flanges in the proposed Topjet toner cartridges lack inward projections, and (ii) limit the basis for its ruling request to the argument that its proposed cartridges have “no projections that are ‘closer together farther from the drum,’ i.e., that project radially inwardly to a greater extent at a positon farther from the cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder.”  See E-mail from David Farnum to William Wittwer, Michael Sandonato, and Edmund Haughey (Feb. 4, 2018).In view of Topjet’s withdrawal of all arguments disputed by Canon and Canon’s clear indication that it does not dispute any of the remaining arguments, no additional briefing or oral argument was needed by CBP in this inter partes proceeding to reach a determination regarding the questions presented in the Ruling Request.  For the reasons discussed below, we hold that the Topjet toner cartridges, i.e., the 217 toner cartridges and the 226 toner cartridges, are not subject to the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.B.  	Investigation No. 337-TA-9181.  	Procedural HistoryThe Commission instituted the ’918 investigation on June 12, 2014, based on a complaint filed by Canon Inc. of Tokyo; Canon U.S.A., Inc. of Melville, New York; and Canon Virginia, Inc. of Newport News, Virginia (collectively, “Canon Complainants”).  See 79 Fed. Reg. 33777 (June 12, 2014).  The Canon Complainants alleged violations by thirty-three respondents of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1337, based upon the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain toner cartridges and components thereof by reason of infringement of certain claims of U.S. Patent No. 8,280,278 (‘‘the ’278 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,630,564 (‘‘the ’564 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,682,215 (‘‘the ’215 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,676,090 (‘‘the ’090 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,369,744 (‘‘the ’744 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,565,640 (‘‘the ’640 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,676,085 (‘‘the ’085 patent’’); U.S. Patent No. 8,135,304 (‘‘the ’304 patent’’); and U.S. Patent No. 8,688,008 (‘‘the ’008 patent’’).  Id. See Notice of a Commission Determination Not To Review an Initial Determination Terminating the Investigation as To U.S. Patent Nos. 8,369,744; 8,565,640; 8,676,085; and 8,135,304, Doc. See ID at 80 – 249, Doc. ID 556964 (May 12, 2015).    On August 31, 2015, the Commission determined to affirm the ALJ’s finding of a violation of section 337, and issued a general exclusion order (“GEO”) barring entry of certain toner cartridges and components thereof that infringe one or more of claims 160, 165, and 166 of the ’278 patent; claims 171, 176, 179, 181, 189, 192, and 200 of the ’564 patent; claims 23, 26, 27, and 29 of the ’215 patent; claims 1–4 of the ’090 patent; and claims 1, 7–9, 11, 12, and 34 of the ’008 patent. The Article at Issue and Arguments Presented to CBPThe articles at issue in the Ruling Request (Figures 6 – 11, below) are the 217 toner cartridges and the 226 toner cartridges.  See Ruling Request  at 10-18.  Topjet provided CBP with samples of the 217 toner cartridge and the 226 toner cartridge for examination.   Topjet asserts that the neither the 217 toner cartridges nor the 226 toner cartridges infringe any of the patents listed in the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation because the toner cartridges lack (i) an inclining coupling member that is a required claim element of certain independent claims at issue, and (ii) a particular flange design required by the remaining independent claim at issue.   Id. at 22-28.First, Topjet states that the 217 and 226 toner cartridges do not possess an inclining coupling member on a separate axis from the developer roller. See RR at 24-25.  Rather, the coupling member is set along the same axis as the drum roller and is perpendicular to the drum-end flange (Figures 7 and 10 below).  Furthermore, the coupling members of both the 217 and 226 toner cartridges engage the drive shaft using a lever system that moves the coupling horizontally along the longitudinal axis of the photosensitive drum or an axis parallel to the longitudinal axis of the developer roller.  Id. Second, Topjet asserts that the flange on the drum units do not have projections that project radially inward to a greater extent at a position farther from the drum cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder (Figures 8 and 11  below).  Id. at 27-28.  Figure 6: Diagram of 217 Cartridge(See RR at 12, Fig. 2)Figure 7: Diagram of 217 Cartridge Coupling(See RR at 13, Fig. 4B)Figure 8: Cross section of 217 Flange (See RR at 14, Fig. 6A)Figure 9: 226 Toner Cartridge(See RR at 15, Fig. 7)Figure 10:  Cross Section View of 226 Cartridge Coupling Mechanism(See RR at 18, Fig. 11B)Figure 11: Cross Section of 226 Flange(See RR at 18, Fig. 12A)Topjet also cited CBP Rulings HQ H280845 (dated Feb. 1, 2017), HQ H272714 (dated July 1, 2016), and HQ H278406 (dated Mar. 6, 2017) in support of its arguments.  See RR at 19.  Topjet argued that the 217 toner cartridges and the 226 toner cartridges are substantially similar to the products in question in these three rulings and accordingly, Topjet concluded that, similar to the holdings in these rulings, the 217 and 226 toner cartridges are outside the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.  Id. An examination by CBP of the sample 217 toner cartridge and drum flanges revealed that the coupling does not pivot, moves only coaxial to the drum unit, and that it is set perpendicular to the flange of the drum unit.  An examination of the diagrams of the 226 toner cartridge, figures 9 and 10 above, reveals that its coupling also does not pivot but moves only coaxial to the drum unit and that it is set perpendicular to the flange of the drum unit.   Lastly, an examination of the cross sectioned drum flange diagrams, figures 8 and 11 above, for the 217 and 226 cartridges  reveals that there projections do not project radially inward to a greater extent at a position farther from the drum cylinder than at a position closer to the cylinder.  Rather, the projections appear to project radially inward the same uniform distance throughout the drum flange, regardless of position relative to the drum cylinder.ISSUE:Whether the 217 toner cartridges and 226 toner cartridges infringe any of claims 160, 165, and 166 of the ’278 patent; claims 171, 176, 179, 181, 189, 192, and 200 of the ’564 patent; claims 23, 26, 27, and 29 of the ’215 patent; claims 1–4 of the ’090 patent; and claims 1, 7–9, 11, 12, and 34 of the ’008 patent, and are therefore within the scope of the GEO issued in the ’918 investigation.LAW AND ANALYSIS:Law of Patent InfringementUnder section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. § 1337, the Commission has authority to conduct investigations into imported articles that allegedly infringe United States patents and impose remedies if the accused articles are found to be infringing. See 19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(1)(B), (b)(1), (d), (f), (i). 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d), in particular, empowers the Commission to direct the exclusion from entry of articles found to infringe the asserted patents. When the Commission determines there is infringement and thus a violation of section 337, it generally issues one of two types of exclusion orders: (1) a limited exclusion order or (2) a general exclusion order. See Fuji Photo Film Co., Ltd. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 474 F.3d 1281, 1286 (Fed. Cir. 2007).Both types of orders direct CBP to bar infringing products from entering the country. See Yingbin-Nature (Guangdong) Wood Indus. Co. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 535 F.3d 1322, 1330 (Fed Cir. 2008). “A limited exclusion order is ‘limited’ in that it only applies to the specific parties before the Commission in the investigation. In contrast, a general exclusion order bars the importation of infringing products by everyone, regardless of whether they were respondents in the Commission's investigation.” Id. See 19 U.S.C. §§ 1337(d)(1) (“The Commission shall notify the Secretary of the Treasury of its action under this subsection directing such exclusion from entry, and upon receipt of such notice, the Secretary shall, through the proper officers, refuse such entry.”); id. at (i)(3) (“Upon the attempted entry of articles subject to an order issued under this subsection, the Secretary of the Treasury shall immediately notify all ports of entry of the attempted importation and shall identify the persons notified under paragraph (1)(C).”) (emphasis added); see also ClearCorrect Operating, LLC v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 810 F.3d 1283, 1295 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (“This section [1337(i)] permits the Commission to exclude ‘articles’ from importation into the United States; however, it is difficult to see how one could physically stop electronic transmissions at the borders under the current statutory scheme…. This section reads, ‘[u]pon the attempted entry of articles subject to an order issued under this subsection, the Secretary of the Treasury shall immediately notify all ports of entry of the attempted importation and shall identify the persons notified under paragraph (1)(C).’ Not only can an electronic transmission not be subject to an ‘attempted entry’ through a ‘port of entry,’ it also cannot be intercepted at a ‘port of entry’ as contemplated in the statute.”) (emphasis added), reh’ng en banc denied by Clearcorrect Operating v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 819 F.3d 1334 (Fed. Cir. 2016).Significantly, unlike district court injunctions, the Commission can issue a general exclusion order that broadly prohibits entry of articles that infringe the relevant claims of an asserted patent without regard to whether the persons importing such articles were parties to, or were related to parties to, the investigation that led to issuance of the general exclusion order. See Vastfame Camera, Ltd. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 386 F.3d 1108, 1114 (Fed. Cir. 2004). The Commission also has recognized that even limited exclusion orders have broader applicability beyond just the parties found to infringe during an investigation. See Certain GPS Devices and Products Containing Same, Inv. No. 337-TA-602, Comm’n Op. at 17, n. 6, Doc ID 317981 (Jan. 2009) (“We do not view the Court’s opinion in Kyocera as affecting the issuance of LEOs [limited exclusion orders] that exclude infringing products made by respondents found to be violating Section 337, but imported by another entity. MercExchange, L.L.C., 547 U.S. 388 (2006), opinion “does not apply to Commission remedy determinations under Section 337.” Spansion, Inc. v. U.S. Int’l Trade Comm’n, 629 F.3d 1331, 1359 (Fed. Cir. 2010). Reels of Super 8mm Film, 413 U.S. 123 (1973) (“Import restrictions and searches of persons or packages at the national borders rest on different considerations and different rules of constitutional law from domestic regulations. Stranahan, 192 U.S. 470 (1904) (“As a result of the complete power of Congress over foreign commerce, it necessarily follows that no individual has a vested right to trade with foreign nations, which is so broad in character as to limit and restrict the power of Congress to determine what articles of merchandise may be imported into this country and the terms upon which a right to import may be exercised.
