Claims 1, 13, 15, and 20 of the ’757 patent   The ’757 patent is titled “Leak-Resistant Vaporizer Device” and describes “[v]aporizer cartridges and vaporizer apparatuses, and methods for making, using and delivering vapor to a 
     8  user, that are leak-resistant for use with cannabinoids.”  ’757 patent at codes (54) and (57).   Claims 1 and 15 are independent claims of the ’757 patent and claims 13 and 20 depend from claims 1 and 15, respectively.  Claims 1 and 15 of the ’757 patent are reproduced below:     1. A vaporizer cartridge comprising [757.1.pre]: a cartridge body comprising a proximal body end and a distal body end opposite the proximal body end [757.1.a]; a mouthpiece coupled to the proximal body end, the mouthpiece comprising an outlet [757.1.b]; a reservoir configured to hold a vaporizable material [757.1.c]; a first pad positioned within an interior of the mouthpiece [757.1.d]; a second pad positioned within the interior of the mouthpiece [757.1.e]; a heater chamber comprising [757.1.f]: a heater configured to heat the vaporizable material from the reservoir to generate an aerosol [757.1.f.i]; a housing piece configured to house at least a portion of the heater, the housing piece comprising a housing opening configured to receive at least a portion of the heater [757.1.f.ii]; an air tube extending from the housing piece [757.1.f.iii]; a bottom cover comprising a bottom portion positioned distally relative to the cartridge body, the bottom portion comprising: a first air opening and a second air opening; and [757.1.g] a distal member positioned at least partially within the cartridge body between the housing piece and the bottom cover, the distal member comprising [757.1.h]: a proximal side [757.1.h.i]; a distal side opposite the proximal side [757.1.h.ii]; a lateral side extending between the proximal side and the distal side; and  [757.1.h.iii] at least one recessed surface positioned on the lateral side [757.1.h.iv]; wherein an air chamber is formed between the distal member and the bottom portion of the bottom cover [757.1.i]; and wherein the first air opening and the second air opening of the bottom portion allow air to pass into the air chamber [757.1.j].   15. A vaporizer device comprising: [757.15.pre] a vaporizer cartridge, comprising [757.15.a]:  a cartridge body comprising a proximal body end and a distal body end opposite the proximal body end [757.15.a.i]; a mouthpiece coupled to the proximal body end, the mouthpiece comprising an outlet [757.15.a.ii]; a reservoir configured to hold a vaporizable material [757.15.a.iii]; a first pad positioned within an interior of the mouthpiece [757.15.a.iv]; a second pad positioned within the interior of the mouthpiece [757.15.a.v]; a heater chamber comprising [757.15.a.vi]: 
     9  a heater configured to heat the vaporizable material from the reservoir to generate an aerosol [757.15.a.vi.a]; a housing piece configured to house at least a portion of the heater, the housing piece configured to receive at least a portion of the heater [757.15.a.vi.b]; a distal member positioned at least partially within the cartridge body between the housing piece and the bottom cover, the distal member comprising [757.15.a.viii]: a proximal side [757.15.a.viii.a]; a distal side opposite the proximal side [757.15.a.viii.b]; a lateral side extending between the proximal side and the distal side; and [757.15.a.viii.c] at least one recessed surface positioned on the lateral side [757.15.a.viii.d]; wherein an air chamber is formed between the distal member and the bottom portion of the bottom cover; and [757.15.a.ix] wherein the first air opening and the second air opening of the bottom portion allow air to pass into the air chamber; [757.15.a.x] a first cartridge electrical contact; and [757.15.a.xi] a second cartridge electrical contact; and [757.15.a.xii] a vaporizer body, comprising:[757.15.b] a cartridge receiver configured to insertably receive the vaporizer cartridge, the cartridge receiver comprising: [757.15.b.i] a first body electrical contact configured to electrically couple to the first cartridge electrical contact of the vaporizer cartridge; [757.15.b.i.a] a second body electrical contact configured to electrically couple to the second cartridge electrical contact of the vaporizer cartridge; [757.15.b.i.b] an insertion end into which the vaporizer cartridge is inserted; and [757.15.b.i.c] a base opposite the insertion end; and [757.15.b.i.d] one or more LEDs, wherein the vaporizer device is configured to cause the one or more LEDs to illuminate during the generation of the aerosol by the heater of the vaporizer cartridge.  [757.15.b.ii]  ’757 patent at 34:30-65 and 36:1-15.    c.  Claims 1, 5, 10-11, 17-18, and 22 of the ’527 patent  The ‘527 patent is titled “Leak-Resistant Vaporizer Device” and describes “[v]aporizer cartridges and vaporizer apparatus, and methods for making, using and delivering vapor to a user, that are leak-resistant for use with cannabinoids.”  ’527 patent at codes (54) and (57).   Claims 1, 11, and 18 of the ’527 patent are independent claims.  Claims 5 and 10 depend from claim 1 and claims 17 and 22 depend from claims 11 and 18, respectively. III. LEGAL FRAMEWORK  A. Section 337 Exclusion Order Administration    The Commission shall investigate any alleged violation of section 337 to determine, with respect to each investigation conducted by it under this section, whether there is a violation of this section.  See 19 U.S.C. § 1337(b)(1) and (c).  If the Commission determines, as a result of an investigation under this section, that there is a violation of this section, it shall direct that the articles concerned, imported by any person violating the provision of this section, be excluded from entry into the United States unless the Commission finds based on consideration of the public interest that such articles should not be excluded from entry.  See 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)(1).    When the Commission determines that there is a violation of section 337, it generally issues one of two types of exclusion orders: (1) a limited exclusion order or (2) a general exclusion order.  See Fuji Photo Film Co., Ltd. v. ITC, 474 F.3d 1281, 1286 (Fed. Cir. 2007).  Both types of orders direct CBP to bar infringing products from entering the country.  See Yingbin-Nature (Guangdong) Wood Indus. Co. v. ITC, 535 F.3d 1322, 1330 (Fed Cir. 2008).  “A limited exclusion order is ‘limited’ in that it only applies to the specific parties before the Commission in the investigation.  In contrast, a general exclusion order bars the importation of infringing products by everyone, regardless of whether they were respondents in the Commission's investigation.”  Id.  A general exclusion order is appropriate only if two exceptional circumstances apply.  See Kyocera Wireless Corp. v. ITC, 545 F.3d 1340, 1356 (Fed. Cir. 2008).  A general exclusion order may only be issued if (1) “necessary to prevent circumvention of a limited exclusion order,” or (2) “there is a pattern of violation of this section and it is difficult to Identify the source of infringing products.”  19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)(2); see Kyocera, 545 F.3d at 1356 (“If a complainant wishes to obtain an exclusion order operative against articles of non-respondents, it must seek a GEO [general exclusion order] by satisfying the heightened burdens of §§ 1337(d)(2)(A) and (B).”).  
     21  In addition to the action taken above, the Commission may issue an order under 19 U.S.C. § 1337(i) directing CBP to seize and forfeit articles attempting entry in violation of an exclusion order if their owner, importer, or consignee previously had articles denied entry on the basis of that exclusion order and received notice that seizure and forfeiture would result from any future attempt to enter articles subject to the same.  An exclusion order under § 1337(d)—either limited or general—and a seizure and forfeiture order under § 1337(i) apply at the border only and are operative against articles presented for customs examination or articles conditionally released from customs custody but still subject to a timely demand for redelivery.  See 19 U.S.C. §§ 1337(d)(1) (“The Commission shall notify the Secretary of the Treasury of its action under this subsection directing such exclusion from entry, and upon receipt of such notice, the Secretary shall, through the proper officers, refuse such entry.”); Id. at (i)(3) (“Upon the attempted entry of articles subject to an order issued under this subsection, the Secretary of the Treasury shall immediately notify all ports of entry of the attempted importation and shall identify the persons notified under paragraph (1)(C).”) (emphasis added).   Significantly, unlike district court injunctions, the Commission can issue a general exclusion order that broadly prohibits entry of articles that violate section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 without regard to whether the persons importing such articles were parties to, or were related to parties to, the investigation that led to issuance of the general exclusion order.  See Vastfame Camera, Ltd. v. ITC, 386 F.3d 1108, 1114 (Fed. Cir. 2004).  The Commission also has recognized that even limited exclusion orders have broader applicability beyond just the parties found to infringe during an investigation.  See Certain GPS Devices and Products Containing Same, Inv. No. 337-TA-602, Comm’n Op. at 17, n.6, Doc ID 317981 (Jan. 2009) (“We do not view the Court’s opinion in Kyocera as affecting the issuance of LEOs [limited exclusion orders] that exclude infringing products made by respondents found to be violating Section 337, but imported by another entity.  The exclusionary language in this regard that is traditionally included in LEOs is consistent with 19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(1)(B)-(D) and 19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)(1).”).    Moreover, “[t]he Commission has consistently issued exclusion orders coextensive with the violation of section 337 found to exist.”  See Certain Erasable Programmable Read Only Memories, Inv. No. 337-TA-276, Enforcement Proceeding, Comm’n Op. at 11, Doc ID 43536 (Aug. 1991) (emphasis added).  “[W]hile individual models may be evaluated to determine importation and [violation], the Commission's jurisdiction extends to all models of [violative] products that are imported at the time of the Commission’s determination and to all such products that will be imported during the life of the remedial orders.”  See Certain Optical Disk Controller Chips and Chipsets, Inv. No. 337-TA-506, Comm’n Op. at 56-57, USITC Pub. 3935, Doc ID 287263 (July 2007).   Lastly, despite the well-established principle that “the burden of proving infringement generally rests upon the patentee [or plaintiff],” Medtronic, Inc. v. Mirowski Family Ventures, LLC, 571 U.S. 191 (2014), the Commission has held that Medtronic is not controlling precedent and does not overturn its longstanding practice of placing the burden of proof on the party who, in light of the issued exclusion order, is seeking to have an article entered for consumption.  See Certain Sleep-Disordered Breathing Treatment Systems and Components Thereof, Inv. No. 337-TA-879, Advisory Opinion at 6-11.  In particular, the Commission has 
     22  noted that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (“Federal Circuit”) “has upheld a Commission remedy which effectively shifted the burden of proof on infringement issues to require a company seeking to import goods to prove that its product does not infringe, despite the fact that, in general, the burden of proof is on the patentee to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that a given article does infringe[.]”  Certain Integrated Circuit Telecommunication Chips, Inv. No. 337-TA-337, Comm’n Op. at 21, n.14, USITC Pub. 2670, Doc ID 217024 (Aug. 1993) (emphasis in original) (citing Sealed Air Corp. v. ITC, 645 F.2d 976, 988-89 (C.C.P.A. 1981)).   This approach is supported by Federal Circuit precedent.  See Hyundai Elecs. Indus. Co. v. ITC, 899 F.2d 1204, 1210 (Fed. Cir. 1990) (“Indeed, we have recognized, and Hyundai does not dispute, that in an appropriate case the Commission can impose a general exclusion order that binds parties and non-parties alike and effectively shifts to would-be importers of potentially infringing articles, as a condition of entry, the burden of establishing noninfringement.  The rationale underlying the issuance of general exclusion orders—placing the risk of unfairness associated with a prophylactic order upon potential importers rather than American manufacturers that, vis-a-vis at least some foreign manufacturers and importers, have demonstrated their entitlement to protection from unfair trade practices—applies here [in regard to a limited exclusion order] with increased force.”) (emphasis added) (internal citation omitted).     B. Patent Infringement    Determining patent infringement requires two steps.  Advanced Steel Recovery, LLC v. X-Body Equip., Inc., 808 F.3d 1313, 1316 (2015).  The first is to construe the limitations of the asserted claims and the second is to compare the properly construed claims to the accused product.  Id.  To establish literal infringement, every limitation recited in a claim must be found in the accused product whereas, under the doctrine of equivalents, infringement occurs when there is equivalence between the elements of the accused product and the claimed elements of the patented invention.  Microsoft Corp. v. GeoTag, Inc., 817 F.3d 1305, 1313 (Fed. Cir. 2016).  One way to establish equivalence is by showing, on an element-by-element basis, that the accused product performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way with substantially the same result as each claim limitation of the patented invention, which is often referred to as the function-way-result test.  See Intendis GmbH v. Glenmark Pharms., Inc., 822 F.3d 1355, 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2016).    As for the first step above, “claim construction is a matter of law.”  SIMO Holdings, Inc. v. H.K. uCloudlink Network Tech., Ltd., 983 F.3d 1367, 1374 (Fed. Cir. 2021).  Moreover, the ultimate construction of a claim limitation is a legal conclusion, as are interpretations of the patent’s intrinsic evidence (the patent claims, specifications, and prosecution history).  UltimatePointer, L.L.C. v. Nintendo Co., 816 F.3d 816, 822 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (citing Teva Pharms. USA, Inc. v. Sandoz, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 831, 841, 190 L. Ed. 2d 719 (2015).  “Importantly, the person of ordinary skill in the art is deemed to read the claim term not only in the context of the particular claim in which the disputed term appears, but in the context of the entire patent, including the specification.”  Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1313 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc).  “In some cases, the ordinary meaning of claim language as understood by a person of 
     23  skill in the art may be readily apparent even to lay judges.”  Id. at 1314.  In others, courts look to public sources such as “the words of the claims themselves, the remainder of the specification, the prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence concerning relevant scientific principles, the meaning of technical terms, and the state of the art.”  Id.    “To begin with, the context in which a term is used in the asserted claim can be highly instructive.”  Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1314 (“To take a simple example, the claim in this case refers to ‘steel baffles,’ which strongly implies that the term ‘baffles’ does not inherently mean objects made of steel.”).  The context in which a claim term is used also includes the full chain of dependence as well as the remaining suite of claims and the written description.  See Inline Plastics Corp. v. EasyPak, LLC, 799 F.3d 1364, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (“Since the specification explicitly mentions the ‘alternative’ . . . there can be no debate concerning the application of the doctrine of claim differentiation.”).      The second step to establish infringement involves a comparison of the claims, as properly construed, to the accused product, which is a question of fact.  Apple Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co., Ltd., 839 F.3d 1034, 1040 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (en banc).      IV. CATEGORY: 19 U.S.C. § 1337; Unfair Competition  Christopher J. Lutz Armis IP Law, L.L.C. P.O. Box 1564 Westborough, MA 01581  VIA EMAIL: chris.lutz@armisiplaw.com   RE: Request for Ruling Reconsideration under 19 CFR § 177.2 and § 177.12; U.S. International Trade Commission; Limited Exclusion Order; Investigation No. 337-TA-1362; Certain Liquid Transfer Devices with an Integral Vial Adapter  Dear Mr. Lutz:   Pursuant to 19 C.F.R. Part 177, the Exclusion Order Enforcement Branch (EOE), Regulations and Rulings, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) issues this letter in response to Summit International Medical Technologies, Inc.’s (“Summit”) Request for Ruling Reconsideration, dated May 15, 2026 (the “Reconsideration Request”) of HQ H347235, dated March 27, 2026 (the “Ruling Letter” or  “underlying Part 177 proceeding”).  In the Ruling Letter, we found that Summit did not meet its burden to show that its redesigned version of liquid transfer device (the “redesigned article”) was not subject to the limited exclusion order (LEO or “1362 LEO”) that the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC or “Commission”) issued as a result of Investigation No. 337-TA-1362 (“the 1362 investigation” or “the underlying investigation”) under Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, 19 U.S.C. § 1337.  For the reasons below, we affirm the Ruling Letter.    Determinations of the Commission resulting from the underlying investigation or a related proceeding under 19 C.F.R. Part 210 are binding authority on CBP and in the case of conflict will, by operation of law, modify or revoke any contrary CBP ruling or decision pertaining to Section 337 exclusion orders.  Should a party disagree with CBP in the Ruling Letter or this response, there are ancillary proceedings available at the ITC.  See 19 CFR 210.75 – 76.   This letter is the result of a request for reconsideration under 19 C.F.R. Part 177 that was conducted on an inter partes basis.  The proceeding involved the two parties with a direct and demonstrable interest in the question presented by the Reconsideration Request: (1) your client, Summit, the Reconsideration Requester and original ruling requester, and respondent in the 1362 
  2  investigation; and (2) West Pharmaceutical Services, Inc. and West Pharma Services, IL, Ltd.  (collectively, “West”), the patent owner and complainant in the 1362 investigation.  See 19 C.F.R. § 177.1(c).   The parties were asked to identify in their submissions confidential information, including information subject to the administrative protective order in the underlying investigation, with [[red brackets]].  See 19 C.F.R. §§ 177.2, 177.8.  Consistent with the above, the parties are directed to identify information in this ruling that should be bracketed in red [[  ]] because it constitutes confidential information, as defined below, such that it should be redacted from the public version of this ruling that will be published in accordance with 19 C.F.R. § 177.10.  The parties are to contact the EOE Branch within ten (10) working days of the date of this ruling letter to identify such information with brackets.  See, e.g., 19 C.F.R. § 177.8(a)(3).    Please note that disclosure of information related to administrative decisions under 19 C.F.R. Part 177 is governed by, for example, 6 C.F.R. Part 5, 31 C.F.R. Part 1, 19 C.F.R. Part 103, and 19 C.F.R. § 177.8(a)(3).  See, e.g., 19 C.F.R. § 177.10(a).  In addition, CBP is guided by the laws relating to confidentiality and disclosure, such as the Freedom of Information Act (“FOIA”), as amended (5 U.S.C. § 552), the Trade Secrets Act (18 U.S.C. § 1905), and the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended (5 U.S.C. § 552a).  A request for confidential treatment of information submitted in connection with a ruling requested under 19 C.F.R. Part 177 faces a strong presumption in favor of disclosure.  See, e.g., 19 C.F.R. § 177.8(a)(3).  The person seeking this treatment must overcome that presumption with a request that is appropriately tailored and supported by evidence establishing that: the information in question is customarily kept private or closely-held and either that the government provided an express or implied assurance of confidentiality when the information was shared with the government or there were no express or implied indications at the time the information was submitted that the government would publicly disclose the information.  See Food Marketing Institute v. Argus Leader Media, 139 S. Ct. 2356, 2366 (2019) (concluding that “[a]t least where commercial or financial information is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner and provided to the government under an assurance of privacy, the information is ‘confidential’ within the meaning of exemption 4.”); see also U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Information Policy (OIP): Step-by-Step Guide for Determining if Commercial or Financial Information Obtained from a Person is Confidential Under Exemption 4 of the FOIA (updated 10/7/2019); see also OIP Guidance: Exemption 4 after the Supreme Court’s Ruling in Food Marketing Institute v. Argus Leader Media (updated October 4, 2019).    I. BACKGROUND  A more detailed description of the background of the underlying investigation, the asserted claims of the patents in the 1362 LEO, the accused products from the underlying investigation, and the procedural history of the instant ruling request, other than the new procedural developments described below, was provided in the Ruling Letter and is adopted herein.  Ruling Letter at 2-14.  The Ruling Letter was issued on March 27, 2026.  The subsequent timeline of events is as follows: 
  3   ? On May 15, 2026, Summit filed the Reconsideration Request. ? On May 18, 2026, the EOE Branch established the schedule for this reconsideration proceeding, which provided West with an opportunity to respond to the Reconsideration Request and set a target date of June 19, 2026, for issuance of the EOE Branch decision.   ? On May 22, 2026, West’s counsel requested a one-week extension of the procedural schedule for personal circumstances.   ? On May 22, 2026, the EOE Branch granted the one-week extension and set a revised target date of June 26, 2026. ? On June 5, 2026, in line with the modified schedule, West provided its response (“West Response”).   ? On June 24, 2026, the EOE Branch modified the schedule and extended the target date to July 8, 2026. ? On July 8, 2026, the EOE Branch further modified the schedule and extended the target date by two days to July 10, 2026.   II. ISSUE  Whether Summit has shown that the Ruling Letter is in error such that it should be revoked or modified under 19 C.F.R. § 177.12(a).   III. LEGAL FRAMEWORK  The legal framework on Section 337 exclusion order administration and patent infringement was discussed in the Ruling Letter and is adopted herein.  Ruling Letter at 14-18.   IV.  ANALYSIS  Revocation or modification of rulings issued under 19 C.F.R. Part 177 are provided for in 19 C.F.R. § 177.12.  19 C.F.R. § 177.12(a) provides in relevant part: “[a]n interpretive ruling . . . issued under this part . . . if found to be in error or not in accord with the current views of Customs, may be modified or revoked by an interpretive ruling issued under this section.”  Moreover, as identified in HQ H328569, dated November 28, 2022, the party requesting reconsideration bears the burden of establishing that the ruling letter is in error:  [U]nder CBP HQ Ruling H284032 (dated April 7, 2017), “[w]hen CBP undertakes review to determine if an issued ruling letter is in error based on a request from a person outside of CBP, the burden to establish that the ruling letter is incorrect, either legally or factually, falls on the person seeking to have that ruling letter modified or revoked.”  HQ H28432  at 39 (emphasis added).  Id. at 8 (emphasis in the original).  Accordingly, Summit, as the party seeking to have the Ruling 
  4  Letter modified or revoked, bears the burden to establish that the Ruling Letter is incorrect either legally or factually.  CBP has reviewed the Ruling Letter and the parties’ arguments in this proceeding and finds that Summit fails to provide any new evidence or legal arguments in the Reconsideration  Request establishing that the Ruling Letter is incorrect either factually or legally.  The seven errors alleged by Summit repeat arguments it previously made that have been addressed in the underlying Part 177 proceeding.  As such, Summit provides no basis for CBP to revoke or modify the Ruling Letter.  Nonetheless, we address these arguments separately below, for the sake of completeness.    A. Summary of Position   Although Summit identifies seven purported errors in the Ruling Letter, each ultimately rests upon the unestablished premise that the mere incorporation of a valve between the integral vial adapter and IV spike necessarily precludes the "direct and continuous fluid communication" required by limitation 1.5 of claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 10,688,295 (“the ’295 patent”).  The EOE Branch carefully considered this argument during the underlying Part 177 proceeding and rejected it because Summit had not established that proposition through the claim language, the Commission's claim construction, the intrinsic record, the evidentiary record, or citing to a controlling authority.  See Ruling Letter at 25-28.  The Ruling Letter identified this deficiency by stating: “the EOE Branch finds that Summit has not met its burden to show that the redesigned product does not practice the ‘direct and continuous fluid communication’ requirement of limitation 1.5 because (1) Summit’s own claim construction of ‘direct’ and ‘continuous’ are inadequate and (2) its dictionary definitions of these terms are inconsistent with the view of the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) that ‘direct and continuous’ can be practiced despite the presence of temporary barriers.”  Ruling Letter at 28.    As the party seeking a ruling that its redesigned article is admissible notwithstanding the 1362 LEO, Summit bears the burden to show non-infringement .  See Id.  at 18-19; Hyundai, 899 F.2d at 1210; Certain Integrated Circuit Telecommunication Chips, Inv. No. 337-TA-337, Comm’n Op. at 21 n.14.  Identifying a structural modification satisfies only part of that burden.  Summit is also required to demonstrate that the identified modification is sufficient to show the redesigned article lacks the required claim limitation 1.5.  See, e.g., Zenith Labs., Inc. v. Bristol Meyers Squibb Co., 19 F.3d 1418, 1423 (Fed. Cir. 1994) (explaining that in an infringement analysis, "the only proper comparison is with the claims of the patent"); see also, Certain Network Devices, Related Software and Components Thereof (I), Inv. No. 337-TA-944 (Enforcement Proceeding), EDIS Doc. ID 619096, Notice of Commission Determination to Review the Final Enforcement Initial Determination in Its Entirety; and on Review to Remand the Investigation in Part to the Presiding Administrative Law Judge (Aug. 4, 2017) (“The final EID includes analysis comparing the redesigned products to products found to infringe in the underlying investigation to conclude that the redesigned products do not infringe the '537 patent.  However, this analysis, while addressing the parties' arguments, does not address the issue of whether the language of the claims reads on the redesigned products.”).  As discussed below, the Reconsideration Request fails to meet this burden.   
  5  A. Alleged Error One: the Ruling Letter Applies an Operational Test to a Structural Limitation  Summit first argues that the Ruling Letter improperly analyzed the redesigned article based upon its operation rather than its structure, stating: Nevertheless, the Ruling relies on whether fluid may flow when the valve is opened.  That reasoning applies a method-based or capability-based analysis to a structural device claim and materially departs from governing Federal Circuit precedent.  Whether fluid happens to flow during operation does not alter the physical structure of the device.   Reconsideration Request at 1-2.  According to Summit, limitation 1.5 is a structural apparatus limitation requiring the integral trifurcated connector body to connect the single IV spike in “direct and continuous fluid communication” with the integral vial adapter, such that the Ruling Letter erred by concluding that the redesigned article satisfies that limitation based upon the condition in which the valve is opened.  Id.  at 2 (“The Redesigned Product includes a permanent valve positioned between the vial adapter and IV spike.  That valve interrupts and regulates the pathway between those structures.  By treating limitation 1.5 as satisfied whenever the valve is opened, the Ruling evaluates a structural requirement based on a transient operational state.”).  Summit contends that because the valve is permanently positioned between the integral vial adapter and IV spike, the redesigned article can never possess the structural relationship required by limitation 1.5.  See Id. In response to this argument, West contends that focusing on the redesigned article’s operation as opposed to structure “was not CBP’s method of analysis or conclusion, nor does Summit cite to any portion of the Ruling that would support that characterization.”  West Response at 4. The EOE Branch does not dispute that claim 1 is an apparatus claim, nor that limitation 1.5 recites a structural relationship between the identified components.  Claim 1 requires, among other things, “the integral trifurcated connector body connecting said single IV spike in direct and continuous fluid communication with said integral vial adapter . . .”  ’295 patent at col. 6: 24-26.  The Ruling Letter did not construe this limitation as a method step nor determine that actual liquid flow must occur for the limitation to be satisfied.  Instead, the Ruling Letter identified the redesigned article as including the addition of a valve, recognized the valve as the principal structural modification, considered Summit’s proposed definitions of “direct” and “continuous,” and determined whether Summit had sufficiently demonstrated that the redesigned article no longer satisfies limitation 1.5.  Id.  at 11-14, 22-28.  That analysis necessarily required the EOE Branch to consider how the valve functions within the claimed fluid pathway.  This consideration, however, does not amount to replacing a structural infringement analysis with an operational one.  Accordingly, Summit’s first argument fails to be persuasive.   B. Alleged Error Two: the Ruling Letter Effectively Applies Capability-Based Reasoning to a Non-Capability Claim 
  6   Summit next argues that “[t]he Ruling acknowledges that the asserted claim is not drafted in capability terms, yet it effectively applies capability reasoning by concluding that the Redesigned Product satisfies limitation 1.5 because it can be operated in a manner that permits fluid flow.”  Reconsideration Request at 2.  According to the Reconsideration Request, authorities such as Intel Corp. v. U.S. International Trade Commission, 946 F.2d 821 (Fed. Cir. 1991), Finjan, Inc. v. Secure Computing Corp., 626 F.3d 1197 (Fed. Cir. 2010), and related decisions, concern apparatus claims expressly reciting capability and therefore do not govern the structural limitation at issue here.  Id.  at 2-3 (“Capability-based or periodic infringement concepts arise in the context of method claims or functionally-triggered claim limitations.  They do not transform a structural apparatus claim into one that is satisfied whenever a user manipulates the device into a temporary operating state.  When limitation 1.5 is properly treated as structural, the presence of an intervening valve precludes a finding of ‘direct and continuous fluid communication.’”).  Summit contends that the Ruling Letter erred by treating limitation 1.5 as though it were satisfied merely because the redesigned article can be operated in a manner that permits fluid flow.  Id.   In response, West asserts that that CBP addressed the argument: Separately, at the end of its opinion, CBP addressed the ‘Capability Claiming Line of Precedent.’  Ruling at 32-33.  CBP expressly stated that its holding (discussed above in Section II.a.) applied to a ‘claim that does not contain capability language.’  Id. at 32.  However, CBP offered a second independent and alternative basis to reject Summit’s Rule 177 request. West Response at 5 (emphasis in original). The EOE Branch agrees that limitation 1.5 is not drafted as a capability limitation and does not recite that the vial adapter and IV spike are merely “capable of” direct and continuous fluid communication, but rather, recites a relationship between identified components of an apparatus.  As West notes, however, the Ruling’s discussion of capability case precedent is not the principal basis upon which the Ruling Letter relies.  Before discussing Intel, Finjan, or related authority, the Ruling Letter analyzed the claim language, Summit’s proposed definitions of “direct” and “continuous,” the redesigned article, the Commission record, and the parties’ competing positions concerning limitation 1.5.  Ruling Letter at 22-28.  It was only after completing that analysis that the Ruling Letter addressed Federal Circuit decisions concerning apparatus claims and alternative modes of operation, because these cases were explicitly discussed by the ALJ in the FID.  Id. at 32–33 (“We note that our analysis above is for an apparatus patent claim that does not contain capability language. The EOE Branch also recognizes that in the FID the ALJ cited a line of cases that is directed towards patents with capability claim language . . . Applying the above capability line of precedent to the redesigned products at issue here . . .”)  The Federal Circuit has recognized in several contexts that infringement of an apparatus claim is not necessarily avoided merely because an accused device may also operate in a non-infringing manner.  See, e.g., Core Wireless Licensing S.A.R.L. v. Apple Inc., 899 F.3d 1356, 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2018) (“Infringement is not avoided merely because a non-infringing mode of operation is possible.”).  The Ruling Letter cited this line of authority in response to Summit’s repeated assertion that because the redesigned valve may exist in a closed condition, limitation 1.5 
  7  necessarily cannot be satisfied.  Ruling Letter at 32-33; Summit Revised Ruling Request at 9 (“Put simply, a claim element reciting ‘direct and continuous fluid communication’ cannot be met by an obstructed channel with a valve that discontinues and terminates fluid flow.”) (emphasis added).  That proposition is distinct from construing limitation 1.5 itself as a capability limitation. The Reconsideration Request does not identify any Commission authority holding that apparatus claims containing structural limitations may never be informed by Federal Circuit precedent discussing apparatus functionality or alternative operating conditions. The EOE Branch recognized that in the FID the ALJ cited a line of cases directed toward patents with capability claim language. Particularly, the ALJ noted “[a] device that infringes only some of the time is still a device that infringes.” FID at 64 (citing Hilgraeve Corp. v. Symanetic Corp., 265 F.3d 1336, 1343 (Fed. Cir., 2001)).  But the Federal Circuit has indicated that this line of reasoning only applies to capability claims. In general, however, the Federal Circuit has established that for infringement of a claim that recites capability and not actual operation, an accused device “need only be capable of operating” in the described mode. Intel Corp. v. U.S. Int'l Trade Comm’n, 946 F.2d 821, 832 (Fed. Cir. 1991). Thus, depending on the claims, “an accused device may be found to infringe if it is reasonably capable of satisfying the claim limitations, even though it may also be capable of noninfringing modes of operation.” Hilgraeve Corp. at 1343; Finjan, Inc. v. Secure Computing Corp., 626 F.3d 1197, 1204 (Fed. Cir. 2010) (emphasis added) (citing Intel Corp., 946 F.2d at 832). Applying the above capability line of precedent to the redesigned products at issue here, we found that the redesigned article does not avoid limitation 1.5’s requirement of a “direct and continuous fluid communication” between the IV spike and integral vial adapter. The Reconsideration Request does not address why the ALJ cited similar authorities during the underlying investigation if, as Summit contends, they are categorically inapplicable.  See Id.  at 32-33; Certain Liquid Transfer Devices With an Integral Vial Adapter, Inv. No. 337-TA-1362, EDIS Doc. ID 816231, Public Final Initial Determination (Mar.  15, 2024) (FID) at 64.  Accordingly, Summit has failed to establish that the EOE Branch erred in referencing this analysis in the Ruling Letter.   C. Alleged Error Three: CBP Failed to Recognize the Evidentiary Record of the Complainant’s Own Expert Witness which Confirms that an Intervening Structure Defeats the Limitation  Summit next argues that the Ruling Letter fails to appreciate the testimony from West’s expert, Dr. Cameron, provided during the underlying Commission investigation.  Reconsideration Request at 3.  According to Summit: Complainant’s own expert testified that direct and continuous communication exists where “there is no obstruction in that path” and “no other structures in between.”  The Ruling expressly adopts that testimony.  As recited in the Ruling (P. 23): “Dr. Cameron testified that the IV spike of each accused product is in direct and continuous fluid communication with the integral vial adapter because the pathway 
  8  between those components has no obstructions or intermediary structures.  Tr.  (Cameron) at 122:11-16” The testimony further states: “There is no obstruction in that path.  It goes straight from the vial adapter to the spike.  There are no other structures in between.  So that’s direct and continuous fluid communication there.”); see also Tr.  (Cameron) at 85:4-9, 123:3-124:3, 198:12-21.” Id.  (emphasis in original). Summit contends that this testimony confirms that the valve in the redesigned article is an intervening structure that defeats limitation 1.5.  Id.  Summit also implies that because this testimony came from West’s own expert, the Ruling Letter erred by declining to treat it as dispositive of the redesigned article’s non-infringement.  See Id.   West argues that the testimony of its expert is entirely consistent with the CBP ruling.  “Dr. Cameron testified ‘direct and continuous’ means ‘no obstructions or intermediary structures.’…CBP held in the Ruling that the Redesigned Product has the claimed ‘direct and continuous’ flow path when the valve is open.”  West Response at 5. The EOE Branch does not read the Ruling Letter as disregarding Dr. Cameron’s testimony, nor that, as Summit claims, it  “expressly adopt[] that testimony.”  Id. Expert testimony may assist in understanding the technology and how a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand the claim language, but expert testimony cannot alter the claim language, override the intrinsic record, or substitute for the Commission’s claim construction.  See Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1318 (Fed. Cir. 2005) (en banc). (“[C]onclusory, unsupported assertions by experts as to the definition of a claim term are not useful to a court.”).  Thus, even if Dr. Cameron described “direct and continuous fluid communication” as involving the absence of obstructions or intermediary structures in the context of the adjudicated products, that testimony does not establish the broader proposition that any valve in any redesigned fluid pathway necessarily avoids limitation 1.5. We note that the distinction between technical evidence and claim scope is particularly relevant here.   The Commission’s determinations in the underlying investigation control the scope of the 1362 LEO, including claim construction and infringement findings adopted in the investigation.  Ruling Letter at 16 - 19.  The EOE Branch’s role in this underlying Part 177 proceeding is to apply those determinations to Summit’s redesigned article.  Id.  Where the Commission did not expressly construe a particular phrase, the EOE Branch may consider, inter alia, the claim language, the intrinsic record, relevant extrinsic evidence, and the Commission record in applying the claim to the redesigned article.  See Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1317-1318.  Dr. Cameron’s testimony may therefore be considered as part of that evidentiary record, but it does not itself define the metes and bounds of the claim, override intrinsic evidence, or impose limitations that the Commission did not adopt.   This argument highlights the inadequacy of Summit’s interpretation of “direct and continuous” with the language of limitation 1.5 itself.  We interpret the claim as requiring that the 
  9  integral trifurcated connector body connect the single IV spike in “direct and continuous fluid communication” with the integral vial adapter without regard to temporality.  ’295 patent claim 1.  Summit has not demonstrated that the claim further requires that such communication exist at every moment throughout the use of the product nor that the pathway must be devoid of valves such as a flow-control mechanisms.  As stated above, notably absent from the claim as well as Summit’s own construction of it is the requirement that fluid communication exist “at all times.”   The Federal Circuit has repeatedly instructed that claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning in view of the intrinsic record, and that limitations should not be imported into the claims absent a clear basis for doing so.  See Phillips 415 F.3d at 1312-24 ; Thorner v. Sony Computer Ent. Am. LLC, 669 F.3d 1362, 1365-66 (Fed. Cir. 2012).  Here, Summit does not identify any portion of the specification, prosecution history, or Commission claim construction establishing that “direct and continuous fluid communication” requires the complete absence of valves or other structures such as a flow-control.  Summit also fails to identify any controlling authority holding that a fluid pathway ceases to be “direct and continuous” merely because that pathway is regulated by a valve.  Rather, as discussed in the Ruling Letter, the ALJ did not construe “direct and continuous” to require that the relevant fluid communication exist at all times or under every device condition, such that any intervening or flow-control structure would necessarily defeat limitation 1.5.  Ruling Letter at 25-28.  In declining to review the ALJ’s claim construction and infringement findings, the Commission also declined to read a perpetual temporal component in  limitation 1.5.  Comm’n Op. at 4; Ruling Letter at 8-9, 25-28.  Yet, Summit extrapolates from Dr. Cameron’s testimony exactly that: accepting the broad proposition that a valve, by definition, destroys direct fluid communication whenever it is located between two components.  Summit does not identify any portion of Dr. Cameron's testimony in which she expressly articulated such a categorical rule, and the EOE Branch recognizes a meaningful distinction between testimony that a particular intermediary may interrupt structural fluid communication is certain circumstances, and testimony that the existence of a valve is dispositively incompatible with the claim language at issue.  Summit’s argument places substantial weight on the phrase “no obstructions or intermediary structures,” but the Reconsideration Request does not adequately explain how those words map onto the claim language.  To reiterate, limitation 1.5 does not expressly recite “no obstructions,” “no intermediary structures” or “no valves,” but recites “direct and continuous fluid communication.”  ’295 patent claim 1.    The  weight  afforded to expert testimony depends upon its relationship to the claim language, the intrinsic record, the Commission’s findings, and the specific accused or redesigned product at issue.  Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1319.  (“In sum, extrinsic evidence may be useful to the court, but it is unlikely to result in a reliable interpretation of patent claim scope unless considered in the context of the intrinsic evidence.”).  Here, the Ruling Letter considered the testimony and Summit’s related arguments but found them insufficient to establish that the redesigned valve necessarily defeats limitation 1.5.  The Reconsideration Request does not demonstrate that this weighing of the record was legally or factually erroneous. In summary, to the extent Summit contends that “direct and continuous fluid communication” should be construed to exclude all valves or flow-control components, it has not adequately supported this position by appeal to the claim language, intrinsic record, Commission determinations, or controlling law.  We decline to allow Dr. Cameron’s expert testimony to fill that gap.  This third argument, therefore, fails to be persuasive.  
  10    D. Alleged Error Four: the Valve is Not Comparable to the Removeable Barriers Addressed in the ITC Record  Summit next argues that the Ruling Letter improperly relied upon the Commission’s analysis of removable barriers, breakaway tabs, roller clamps, and sealing membranes in the underlying investigation.  Reconsideration Request at 4-5 (“The Ruling analogizes the valve to removable barriers discussed in the ITC proceeding, including breakaway tabs and sealing membranes.  That comparison does not apply.”).  According to Summit, those structures are materially different from the redesigned valve because they are “temporary or removeable barriers that were effectively outside the operative structure at the point relevant to infringement,” whereas the redesigned valve is “a permanent structural component that remains in the fluid pathway.”  Id.  at 4.  Summit therefore contends that the Ruling Letter erred by analogizing the valve to structures that the Commission considered in a different factual context.  Id.  According to West:  CBP correctly found the ALJ’s reasoning instructive to the Redesigned Product.  Id. at 26.  It found that when the valve is open, the Redesigned Product has the claimed “direct and continuous” flow path configuration.  Id. at 27.  That the valve in the Redesigned Product is a permanent structure is irrelevant to the analogy.  With both the  valve and the tab/membrane, the user alters the structure of the device…into an infringing product.   West Response at 6. As an initial matter, the EOE Branch does not dispute the factual distinction identified by Summit: a valve that remains physically present in the redesigned article differs from a breakaway tab, removable membrane, or other structure that may be removed or altered during preparation for use.  The Ruling Letter did not hold otherwise, and Summit's argument mischaracterizes the purpose for which the Ruling Letter discussed those portions of the FID.  The ALJ’s analysis of removable barriers was relevant not because those structures are identical to the valve in the redesigned article, but because the ALJ did not adopt the categorical proposition advanced by Summit that any permanent structure affecting fluid flow necessarily defeats “direct and continuous fluid communication.”  Ruling Letter at 26-28.  The Ruling Letter cited the FID as instructive because the ALJ considered arguments concerning barriers in the fluid pathway and nevertheless found that the accused products satisfied the relevant limitations.  Id.  That analysis was relevant to the extent it showed that limitation 1.5 had not been construed to impose the absolute, at all-times, no-intervening-structure requirement that Summit advances.  A party may identify factual differences between the adjudicated products and redesigned article, but those differences matter only to the extent they are sufficient to show that the redesigned article does not satisfy at least one required claim limitation.  Summit identifies a factual distinction between removable barriers and a permanent valve but does not carry its burden in establishing why this distinction compels the conclusion that the redesigned article lacks “direct and continuous fluid communication.”  The fact that the redesigned valve differs from temporary barriers does not establish that the valve necessarily defeats limitation 1.5. 
  11  Additionally, we note that neither the Commission nor the ALJ established a bright-line rule that the construction of “direct and continuous” turns solely on the permanence or non-permanence of a potential intervening structure.  Ruling Letter at 26-28.  In other words, the fact that the Commission found certain removable or alterable structures insufficient to avoid infringement does not mean that any permanent structure must avoid infringement.  Such reasoning would invert the Commission’s findings, which were limited to the evidence currently before it. In conclusion, the Ruling Letter expressly described the valve and its position in the fluid pathway and recognized Summit’s argument that the valve constituted an intervening structure between the vial adapter and IV spike.  Id. at 11-14, 25-28.  The EOE Branch then concluded that Summit had not shown that the presence of that valve removed the redesigned article from the scope of limitation 1.5.  Id.  Summit may disagree with that conclusion, but that does not amount  tothe Ruling Letter having erred in finding the Commission’s analysis of removable barriers, breakaway tabs, roller clamps, and sealing membranes, in the underlying investigation to be instructive in analyzing the redesigned article.  The Ruling Letter considered the Commission’s analysis as part of the broader claim-construction and infringement framework governing this proceeding.  Id.  at 25-28.  Accordingly, the Ruling Letter did not fail to distinguish the redesigned article from the article adjudicated in the underlying investigation.   E. Alleged Error Five: Structural Comparison of the Claimed Device and the Redesigned Article is Visually Apparent  Summit next argues that “[t]he structural distinction between the ’295 patent and the Redesigned Product is visually apparent,” and thus confirms that the redesigned article do not satisfy limitation 1.5.  Reconsideration Request at 5-6.  According to Summit, the claimed configuration places the vial adapter and IV spike in direct and continuous fluid communication, whereas the redesigned article  “…introduce[] a permanent valve between the vial adapter and IV spike.”  Id.  at 6.  Summit contends that this structural comparison demonstrates that the redesigned article contains an intervening component that permanently interrupts the required fluid communication.  Id.  Summit therefore argues that the Ruling Letter failed to give effect to the structural differences between the redesigned article and the claimed invention.  See Id. In response, West contends that “that argument is not relevant, because all that matters to infringement is whether the Redesigned Product satisfies the structural limitations of claim 1.”  West Response at 6. The EOE Branch again disagrees with Summit’s proposition, based on the reasoning discussed in response to Alleged Errors One through Four.  Incorporating the responses here, Summit has not established that the Ruling Letter failed to give effect to the structural differences between the redesigned article and the claimed invention. F. Alleged Error Six: the Redesigned Article Requires Independent Application of the Claim  Summit next argues that the Ruling Letter improperly “extends findings concerning different products without fully accounting for the structural differences presented by the 
  12  Redesigned Product” and that while the Commission’s claim construction remains controlling, the EOE Branch was required to independently apply claim 1 to the redesigned article.  Reconsideration Request at 6 – 7.  Summit contends that the Ruling Letter failed to do so because it relied on findings concerning adjudicated products that did not include the redesigned valve.  See Id. West responds that “[t]here is no evidence to support Summit’s argument that CBP failed to consider any structural distinctions between the Redesigned Product and original products when applying the Commission’s claim constructions and findings.”  West Response at 7. An analysis of a redesign does not require the EOE Branch to disregard the Commission’s prior determinations or undertake an infringement analysis as though the Commission investigation had never occurred.  In fact, as “the Commission has paramount authority and responsibility under section 337 of the Tariff Act,” “[i]ts opinion and resultant orders have set the substantive law of [the] case, and its post-hearing submission” add to that law.  See, Eaton Corp. v. United States, 29 C.I.T. 1149, 1164-65 (2005).  The task of the EOE Branch is to independently evaluate the redesigned article, specifically taking into account its difference from the article at issue in the underlying investigation, and analyzing the relevance of the differences and their applications under the Commission’s established claim construction and infringement findings.  The Ruling Letter did just that; it described the redesign in detail, including the incorporation and location of the valve, the revised instructions for use, and the parties’ competing descriptions of the redesigned article, and devoted substantial analysis to evaluating Summit’s contention that the valve removed the redesigned article from the scope of limitation 1.5.  Ruling Letter  at 22-28.  Accordingly, the Ruling Letter independently analyzed the redesigned article such that Summit’s sixth argument fails to be persuasive.    G. Alleged Error Seven: the Ruling Risks Reading the Limitation Out of the Claim  Finally, Summit argues that the interpretation adopted in the Ruling Letter effectively reads the “direct and continuous fluid communication” limitation out of claim 1.  Reconsideration Request at 7-8.  (“[T]he Ruling risks depriving that limitation of meaningful effect.”).  Summit asserts that “[u]nder the Ruling’s reasoning, any intervening valve or flow-control structure would satisfy the limitation so long as it can be opened.”  Id.  at 7.  According to Summit, if limitation 1.5 is satisfied notwithstanding the incorporation of a valve between the vial adapter and IV spike, then the limitation no longer meaningfully distinguishes the claimed invention from structures lacking the required fluid communication.  Id.  Summit therefore contends that the Ruling Letter’s interpretation deprives limitation 1.5 of operative effect.  See Id. West responds that “Summit rehashes its argument from the Rule 177 proceeding that a finding of infringement reads the ‘direct and continuous’ limitation out of the claim.  CBP heard that argument and properly rejected it.  CBP arrived at the opposite conclusion—that Summit was attempting to improperly import into the claim an “all the time” requirement.  Ruling at 26-27.  CBP rejected that attempt based on a thorough analysis of claim construction evidence.  Id. at 25-27.”  West Response at 7. As a general proposition, every claim limitation must be given meaning and effect.  Bicon, Inc. v. Straumann Co., 441 F.3d 945, 950 (Fed. Cir. 2006) (“Claims are interpreted with an eye 
  13  toward giving effect to all terms in the claim.”).  The EOE Branch likewise agrees that limitation 1.5 cannot be construed so broadly that the requirement of “direct and continuous fluid communication” ceases to impose any meaningful limitation upon claim scope.  The Reconsideration Request, however, does not demonstrate that the Ruling Letter disregarded limitation 1.5.  The Ruling Letter expressly analyzed the language of limitation 1.5, considered the parties’ competing interpretations of the terms “direct” and “continuous,” accepted Summit’s proposed ordinary-meaning definitions for purposes of analysis, evaluated the redesigned article, and decided whether Summit had demonstrated that the redesigned article fell outside the scope of that limitation.  Ruling Letter at 22-28.  This amounts to the EOE Branch having construed and applied limitation 1.5, rather than disregarding it.  We agree with West that this argument was posed and evaluated in the Ruling Letter.  Throughout the underlying Part 177 proceeding, Summit proposed that "direct" means "without intervening factors or intermediaries" and that "continuous" means "marked by uninterrupted extension in space, time, or sequence."  Summit Post-Oral Discussion Submission at 8-10; Ruling Letter at 25.  The EOE Branch accepted those proposed definitions for purposes of its analysis.  Ruling Letter at 26 ("[T]he EOE Branch will adopt and apply Summit's definitions of 'direct' and 'continuous' to the redesigned articles at issue.").  Having adopted Summit's definitions, the Ruling Letter concluded that Summit's own infringement analysis was unsuccessful if incorporating those definitions.  Specifically, Summit's non-infringement argument assumed that "continuous" necessarily means "continuous at all times," notwithstanding that the claim language imposing no such temporal requirement.  Id.  at 26-27.  Summit’s provided definition may include a temporal component, but it does not impose an at all-times temporal requirement that Summit’s non-infringement argument relies upon.  The EOE Branch stated as much in the Ruling Letter:  In fact, the same dictionary Summit cites, Merriam-Webster Dictionary, provides an example sentence in which the term is used that contradicts Summit’s assertions: “The batteries provide enough power for up to five hours of continuous use.”  See Merriam-Webster Online Dictionary, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/continuous (last visited March 17, 2026) (emphasis added).  That is, according to Merriam-Webster, “continuous” does not have a connotation of “all the time” and can be achieved during a limited time period.  Id.  (emphasis added).  This illustrates that under Summit’s theory of non-infringement, “continuous” has no endpoint, which would require reading additional limitations into the claim.  Summit’s argument tries to convert “continuous” into “permanently open” or “uninterrupted at every moment” in the article’s lifetime usage, but those too are further limitations unsupported by the plain language of the claim.  The EOE Branch finds that Summit again reverses the proper claim-construction inquiry and rather than demonstrating that the Ruling Letter eliminates language from limitation 1.5, Summit's argument seeks to incorporate limitations that do not appear in the claim itself.  The Federal Circuit has cautioned against importing additional restrictions into claims absent a clear basis in the intrinsic record.  See Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1320-24, citing Thorner, 669 F.3d at 1365-66 (“(there is sometimes a fine line between reading a claim in light of the specification, and reading a limitation into the claim from the specification.”).?  The proposed interpretation in 
14 the Reconsideration Request does exactly that.  Accordingly, we are unpersuaded that the Ruling Letter reads the limitation out of claim 1.5. V.HOLDINGFor the reasons set forth above, the EOE Branch finds that Summit has failed to meet itsburden in demonstrating the Ruling Letter is in error.  Accordingly, the EOE Branch denies Summit’s Reconsideration and affirms the Ruling Letter, HQ H347235.   
Sincerely,
 Alaina van Horn Chief, Intellectual Property Enforcement Branch / Exclusion Order Enforcement Branch CC:  Domingo M. LLagostera Blank Rome LLP 717 Texas Ave., Suite 1400 Houston, TX 77002 VIA EMAIL:  domingo.llagostera@blankrome.com Alaina van Horn

H334131  
July 23, 2026
  OT:RR:CTF:FTM  H334131 LPO  
CATEGORY: Classification  
TARIFF NO.: 1404.90.90
  Mr. Cesar Augusto Sanchez Gutierrez International Trade Brokers and Forwarders 2261 NW 66th Ave #221 Miami, FL 33122  RE: Classification of Dried Hemp Flowers (Cannabis sativa L.)    Dear Mr. Gutierrez:  This letter is in response to your April 5, 2023 request, on behalf, Health Green S.A.S. (hereinafter, “Health Green”), for a binding ruling regarding the tariff classification under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (“HTSUS”) of hemp flowers (Cannabis sativa L.).  This ruling request was forwarded to this office from the National Commodity Specialist Division for a response.  At the request of Health Green, we met on December 11, 2024, at which time the characteristics of the product and general rulings process were discussed.  Subsequently, on April 22, 2025, in response to our request for additional information on how the hemp flowers are processed, the original submission was supplemented with a detailed description of postharvest processing of the hemp plant.  Our ruling is set forth below.   FACTS:   The merchandise at issue concerns two varieties of hemp flowers exported from Colombia.  In their condition as imported, the subject hemp flowers are dried, de-stemmed, de-leaved, and ground.  Once harvested, the hemp plants are placed in a dehydrator until they reach a final humidity level of 10-15%, after which branches are cut from the buds, leaves are removed from the buds, and the buds are processed in a grinder resulting in 4-millimeter particles.  There are two varieties of the subject ground hemp flower, which Health Green markets as “Mallwa” and “Puka Yana.”  You stated that the primary use for the product at issue is the extraction of CBD oil for the derivative hemp market.  ISSUE:  What is the tariff classification of the subject dried hemp flowers? 
2   LAW AND ANALYSIS:  Classification of goods under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (“HTSUS”) is governed by the General Rules of Interpretation (“GRI”).  GRI 1 provides that classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings of the tariff schedule and any relative section or chapter notes.  In the event that the goods cannot be classified solely on the basis of GRI 1, and if the headings and legal notes do not otherwise require, the remaining GRIs 2 through 6 may then be applied in order.    The HTSUS provisions at issue are as follows:  1404 Vegetable products not elsewhere specified or included. * * * 5302 True hemp (Cannabis sativa L.), raw or processed but not spun; tow and waste of true hemp (including yarn waste and garnetted stock).  Note 1(c) to Section XI, HTSUS, which includes Chapter 53, states that the section does not cover cotton linters or other vegetable materials of Chapter 14.   Note 1 to Chapter 14, HTSUS, states:   This chapter does not cover the following products which are to be classified in section XI: vegetable materials or fibers of vegetable materials of a kind used primarily in the manufacture of textiles, however prepared, or other vegetable materials which have undergone treatment so as to render them suitable for use only as textile materials.  The Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System Explanatory Notes (“ENs”) constitute the official interpretation of the HTSUS.  While not legally binding or dispositive, the ENs provide a commentary on the scope of each heading of the HTSUS and are generally indicative of the proper interpretation of these headings at the international level.  See T.D. 89-80, 54 Fed. Reg. 35127 (August 23, 1989).    The General EN to Chapter 14, states. in pertinent part, that:  The Chapter excludes vegetable materials of a kind used primarily in the manufacture of textiles, however prepared, and other vegetable materials processed for use as textile materials (Section XI).   The General EN to Section XI states, in pertinent part, that:  In general, Section XI covers raw materials of the textile industry (silk, wool, cotton, man-made fibres, etc.), semi-manufactured products (such as yarns and woven fabrics) and the made up articles made from those products.  However, it excludes a certain number of materials and products such as those mentioned in 
3  Note 1 to Section XI, the Notes to certain Chapters or in the following Explanatory Notes on headings in the Section.   The General EN to Chapter 53 provides, in pertinent part, that:  In general, and with certain exceptions referred to in the Explanatory Note to heading 53.05, this Chapter deals with vegetable textile materials (other than cotton) at the various stages from the raw materials to their transformation into woven fabrics.  Before determining whether the subject merchandise is excluded from Section XI by operation of Note 1(c), supra, we first determine whether it is falls under the scope of the exclusion set forth in Note 1 to Chapter 14, supra, i.e., whether it constitutes “vegetable materials or fibers of vegetable materials of a kind used primarily in the manufacture of textiles.”  In this respect, the General EN to Chapter 53 explains that this chapter provides for vegetable textile materials, in various stages between raw plant material and its transformation into woven textile fabric.  Based on your submission, the subject dried, de-stemmed, de-leaved, and ground hemp flower is not a hemp product used as a textile or used to create textile articles.  The part of the hemp plant broadly used for textiles is the bast fibers, which are found in the outer portion of the stalk.1  These fibers from the stalk have the most desired properties for textile production, such as length and strength.  The subject hemp flower, by contrast, does not contain such properties and is not preferred for textile manufacturing.  Thus, the subject dried, ground hemp flower does not constitute vegetable materials of a kind used primarily in the manufacture of textiles.  As such, it is not excluded from classification in Chapter 14 by operation of Note 1 to that Chapter.   You contend that the hemp flower product at issue should be classified in subheading 1404.90.90, HTSUS, which provides for “Vegetable products not elsewhere specified or included… Other: Other,” explaining that the product is akin to the subject of CBP New York Ruling Letter (“NY”) N305504, dated August 28, 2019, which addressed shredded, dried, ground, and pelletized hemp leaves that were imported principally for the extraction of CBD oil.  In NY N305504, CBP determined that the hemp leaf product was classified under heading 1404, HTSUS.  You further suggest that the instant hemp flower product is similar to the “hemp biomass” classified under heading 1404, HTSUS, in NY N339899, dated May 16, 2024.  We note that in the hemp farming industry, hemp biomass generally refers to the stalks, leaves, and other plant matter that remains after the flowers are harvested,2 but can also be obtained by shredding the entire hemp plant to create a homogenous “biomass.”3  It is also important to  1 Dr. Allison P. Young, Fact Sheet: Hemp Fibers and Fabrics Kentucky State, University Cooperative Extension (2020), https://www.kysu.edu/documents/school-of-agriculture-communities-and-the-environment/fcs_hempfibersandfabrics_fs20_accessible.pdf (Last visited July 15, 2026). 2  See Mudassar Hussain et al., Valorization of Hemp Biomass Through Green Methods: A Sustainable Approach for Next-Generation Food Packaging, 165 Trends in Food Science & Technology (2025), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tifs.2025.105295 (last visited July 15, 2026). 3 See Remediation and Disposal Guidelines for Hemp Growing Facilities U.S. Domestic Hemp Production Program, U.S. Department of Agriculture (2021), https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/HempRemediationandDisposalGuidelines.pdf (last visited , July 15, 2026). 
4  clarify that hemp flowers are found on female hemp plants, which are composed of the following parts: the cola, pistils, bracts, trichomes, sugar leaves, fan leaves, stem, branches and roots.  The cola is the flowering portion of the plant, which contains cannabinoids and terpenes, the compounds currently most sought after for those growing for hemp extractions.4  One type of cannabinoid is cannabidiol oil (hereinafter “CBD”).  Cannabinoids such as CBD are found in the highest concentration in the flower portion of the plant but can also be extracted from the stem and leaves.5        CBP has previously considered the classification of other various hemp products under heading 1404, HTSUS.  See Headquarters Ruling Letter (“HQ”) H319673, dated March 30, 2023 (Wherein CBP classified hemp wraps made of hemp flour, taro flour, and adhesive, containing no THC, for use with non-tobacco herbal smoking mixtures, under heading 1404, HTSUS); see also, NY N324505, dated March 18, 2022 (regarding hulls of hemp seeds to be used as an ingredient in snack foods which CBP classified under heading 1404, HTSUS).  Based on the foregoing, we find that the subject hemp flower falls under the scope of heading 1404, HTSUS.    In summary, given that subject hemp flower is not “of a kind used primarily in the manufacture of textiles,” it is not excluded from Chapter 14 by operation of Note 1 to that Chapter.  Because it falls under the scope of heading 1404, HTSUS, it is excluded from classification under Section XI by operation of Note 1(c) to that Section.      HOLDING:  By application of GRIs 1 and 6, the dried hemp flower products are classified in heading 1401, HTSUS, and specifically subheading 1404.90.90, HTSUS, which provides for: “Vegetable products not elsewhere specified or included… Other: Other: Other.”  The column one general rate of duty is free.   This ruling does not address the applicability of any additional duties that may apply to the goods discussed herein. Likewise, duty rates are provided for your convenience and are subject to change. The text of the most recent HTSUS and the accompanying duty rates are provided at www.usitc.gov.  Please note that 19 C.F.R. § 177.9(b)(1) provides that “[e]ach ruling letter is issued on the assumption that all of the information furnished in connection with the ruling request and incorporated in the ruling letter, either directly, by reference, or by implication, is accurate and complete in every material aspect.  The application of a ruling letter by a CBP field office to the transaction to which it is purported to relate is subject to the verification of the facts incorporated in the ruling letter, a comparison of the transaction described therein to the actual transaction, and the satisfaction of any conditions on which the ruling was based.”   4 Lauren McGue, Marysia Morawska, Maurice L. Robinson, and Anegla O’Callaghan, Hemp Basics: Anatomy of a Female Hemp Plant.  University of Nevada, Reno Extension, https://naes.agnt.unr.edu/PMS/Pubs/2021-4479.pdf (last visited July 15, 2026). 5 Floral Hemp: From the Field and Greenhouse to CBD, USDA (2022),  https://www.usda.gov/about-usda/news/blog/2022/02/24/floral-hemp-field-and-greenhouse-cbd (last visited July 15, 2026). 
5  A copy of this ruling letter should be attached to entry documents filed at the time the goods are entered.  If the documents have been filed without a copy, this ruling should be brought to the attention of the CBP officer handling the transaction.        
Sincerely,
      Gregory Connor, Interim Chief Food, Textiles, and Marking Branch
